  • Assuming a speaking‑order is satisfied by a generic “disposed” note – the Supreme Court in Rajesh Gautam requires reasoned findings linked to each allegation.
  • Confusing Algorithmic Transparency Registers with model‑card documentation – ATRs are statutory, machine‑readable, and publicly accessible; model cards are internal technical artefacts.
  • Overlooking the four‑fifths rule when reporting bias metrics – the CVC 2021 circular makes this the benchmark for disparate impact in public‑sector ADMS.
  • Neglecting the requirement for a community‑representative on Mental Health Resource Audit Committees – the MHCA §31 read with the 2021 NHRC advisory mandates lived‑experience participation.
  • Failing to cite the 2023 MeitY Responsible AI Guidelines when arguing for ATR compliance – the guidelines are the operative policy instrument for public‑sector AI governance.
The sections above give you a repeatable, statute‑backed method to dissect any GS IV case study with precision and depth.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Emergency Medical Resources during Pandemics

The allocation of scarce medical resources — oxygen, ventilators, antiviral drugs, and intensive‑care beds — during a pandemic tests the constitutional guarantee of the right to health under Article 21 and the statutory framework of the Disaster Management Act 2005 and the Epidemic Diseases Act 1897. The Supreme Court in Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal (1996) held that the state must provide adequate medical facilities, and in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) it directed equitable oxygen distribution based on a transparent formula. A repeatable case‑study method proceeds through four steps: stakeholder mapping, option generation, constitutional‑statutory testing, and a defensible decision with monitoring.

Stakeholder Mapping

  • Central and state health ministries (policy authority)
  • District collectors and municipal commissioners (operational command)
  • Public‑hospital directors and private‑hospital associations (service providers)
  • Frontline clinicians and nursing staff (clinical judgment)
  • Patient‑advocacy groups and organisations representing vulnerable populations (elderly, immunocompromised, informal‑sector workers)
  • National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) and State Disaster Management Authorities (SDMAs) (coordination)
  • Judiciary (high courts and Supreme Court) (oversight via writ jurisdiction)

Option Generation

  1. First‑come‑first‑served (FCFS) – simple but ignores clinical urgency and equity.
  2. Clinical‑severity triage (SOFA/APACHE scores) – aligns with medical necessity but may disadvantage groups with limited prior access to diagnostics.
  3. Weighted‑equity formula – combines clinical severity, vulnerability index (age, comorbidity, socioeconomic status), and geographic equity (per‑capita bed availability).
  4. Lottery among clinically eligible patients – satisfies procedural fairness when resources are absolutely insufficient.

Constitutional‑Statutory Tests

Each option is examined against (a) Proportionality — the measure must be suitable, necessary, and the least restrictive means to achieve the legitimate aim of saving maximum lives; (b) Non‑discrimination under Articles 14 and 15 — no arbitrary classification based on caste, gender, or economic status; (c) Procedural fairness — transparent criteria, published guidelines, and an appeal mechanism within 24 hours; (d) Accountability — real‑time dashboards audited by the CAG and periodic reports to the NDMA.

Defensible Decision

The weighted‑equity formula (Option 3) supplemented by a 24‑hour clinical review board and a public grievance portal satisfies all four tests. It is proportionate because it targets the most urgent clinical needs while correcting systemic access gaps; it is non‑discriminatory as the vulnerability index is based on objectively verifiable indicators; it provides procedural fairness through published algorithms and an expedited appeal; and it embeds accountability via mandatory data uploads to the NDMA dashboard and quarterly CAG audit. The decision is documented in a speaking order referencing the Disaster Management Act § 12, the NDMA “National Guidelines for Management of Pandemic” (2021), and the Supreme Court directions in the Karnataka oxygen case.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Remote Sensing Data for Land‑Use Planning

Remote‑sensing data from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) underpins decisions on forest diversion, mining leases, urban expansion, and infrastructure corridors. The legal scaffold includes the Land Acquisition Act 2013 (Sections 2‑4 on social impact assessment), the Forest Rights Act 2006 (Section 4 on community forest rights), the National Remote Sensing Policy 2020 (data‑sharing and licensing clauses), and the Supreme Court judgment in Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) which mandated participatory environmental appraisal. Ethical governance requires that satellite‑derived layers — land‑cover change, slope stability, water‑body extent — are not treated as infallible technical facts but as evidence subject to verification, community consent, and proportionality analysis.

Stakeholder Mapping

  • Revenue and planning departments (data requestors)
  • Forest department and wildlife authorities (custodians of protected areas)
  • Tribal gram sabhas and forest‑dwelling communities (rights holders under FRA)
  • ISRO/NRSC (data providers, custodians of calibration metadata)
  • Independent scientific institutions (e.g., IITs, ICAR) for ground‑truthing
  • Civil‑society watchdogs and environmental NGOs (public interest litigants)
  • Judiciary (high courts, National Green Tribunal) (review of procedural compliance)

Option Generation

  1. Open‑access release of raw imagery — maximises transparency but risks misinterpretation and privacy violations for settlements.
  2. Restricted‑access portal with role‑based authentication — limits misuse but may impede community participation.
  3. Co‑produced validated layers — joint ground‑truthing by revenue officials, forest officers, and gram sabha representatives; results published as vetted GIS layers with metadata.
  4. Independent third‑party audit of classification algorithms — engages academic labs to assess accuracy, bias (e.g., systematic under‑detection of shifting cultivation), and uncertainty quantification.

Constitutional‑Statutory Tests

Options are weighed against (a) Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) under FRA § 4 and the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996; (b) Proportionality — the depth of data sharing must be proportionate to the planning objective; (c) Data‑quality accountability — the NRSC’s calibration reports and the CAG’s 2022 audit of “Satellite‑Based Land‑Use Monitoring” require documented error matrices; (d) Environmental justice — the NGT’s “polluter pays” principle extends to data‑driven decisions that disproportionately affect marginalised communities.

Defensible Decision

Adopt Option 3 (co‑produced validated layers) complemented by Option 4 (independent algorithm audit). The workflow: (i) revenue department requests specific thematic layers; (ii) NRSC supplies calibrated imagery with metadata; (iii) joint field teams conduct ground‑truthing within 30 days; (iv) validated layers are uploaded to a public GIS portal under a Creative Commons Attribution‑NonCommercial licence; (v) an annual audit report by an empaneled academic institution is submitted to the NGT and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. This satisfies FPIC, ensures data quality, respects proportionality, and creates an auditable trail for judicial review.

Stakeholder‑Option‑Test Matrix Technique
A state government proposes to allocate a 500‑hectare forest block for a solar park. Satellite data shows 12 % canopy loss over five years. The gram sabha claims customary rights. Using the matrix, identify the defensible option.
Step 1 – Stakeholders: Forest Department, Renewable Energy Agency, Gram Sabha, Tribal Welfare Ministry, NRSC, NGT. Step 2 – Options: (a) Approve based on satellite loss metric alone; (b) Reject outright citing FRA; (c) Conduct joint ground‑truthing, assess alternative sites, and obtain gram sabha consent; (d) Defer decision pending a full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). Step 3 – Tests: Proportionality (c) balances climate goal with rights; Non‑discrimination (c) respects FRA; Procedural fairness (c) includes consent; Accountability (c) creates documented verification. Decision: Option c with a 60‑day joint verification deadline, alternative‑site analysis, and a speaking order referencing FRA § 4, Land Acquisition Act § 2, and NGT precedent.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study mixes technical data (satellite, algorithmic outputs) with rights‑based claims, first sketch the Stakeholder‑Option‑Test matrix on the rough sheet. Fill stakeholders in 30 seconds, list 3‑4 options in 40 seconds, then apply the four constitutional‑statutory tests as column headers. The option that clears all columns becomes your answer core; cite the exact statutory sections and the latest Supreme Court/NGT direction. This structure prevents omission of procedural‑fairness or accountability arguments that examiners reward.

Applying the Principle of Non‑Discrimination in Public‑Sector AI Procurement

Public‑sector procurement of artificial‑intelligence systems — whether for tax‑fraud detection, beneficiary targeting, or predictive policing — must comply with the non‑discrimination guarantee of Articles 14, 15 and 16 of the Constitution, the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order 2017, and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) “Responsible AI Guidelines” 2023. The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) 2021 circular on bias‑impact metrics (four‑fifths rule) operationalises disparate‑impact analysis for automated decision‑making systems (ADMS). A case‑study framework therefore integrates constitutional law, procurement rules, and technical standards.

Stakeholder Mapping

  • Procuring entity (ministry, department, or public‑sector undertaking)
  • Vendor consortium (original equipment manufacturer, system integrator, data‑lab)
  • End‑users (tax officers, welfare administrators, police units)
  • Affected citizens (taxpayers, welfare beneficiaries, communities subject to surveillance)
  • Central Vigilance Commission (oversight of corruption and bias)
  • MeitY (policy steward for AI governance)
  • Judiciary (high courts, Supreme Court) — writ jurisdiction for fundamental‑rights violations

Option Generation

  1. Mandatory pre‑deployment bias audit — independent third‑party evaluates training data, model performance across protected groups (gender, caste, disability, region) using the four‑fifths rule; results published in the Algorithmic Transparency Register.
  2. Diversity‑clause in Request for Proposal (RFP) — requires vendor to demonstrate inclusive development teams and stakeholder‑consultation logs.
  3. Conditional award with post‑deployment monitoring — contract includes quarterly drift‑detection reports and a kill‑switch if disparate impact exceeds threshold.
  4. Exemption for strategic‑technology procurements — argues national‑security or sovereign‑capability grounds to bypass bias audit.

Constitutional‑Statutory Tests

Each option is tested against (a) Equality before law (Art. 14) — the procurement criterion must not create arbitrary classification; (b) Prohibition of discrimination (Art. 15) — no direct or indirect exclusion of protected groups from benefits or burdens of the AI system; (c) Equality of opportunity in public employment (Art. 16) — relevant when AI screens candidates for government jobs; (d) Proportionality — the least restrictive means to achieve the legitimate aim (e.g., revenue protection) while safeguarding non‑discrimination; (e) Procedural fairness — transparent RFP, reasoned award, and an accessible grievance redressal mechanism under the CVC’s 2021 bias‑impact circular.

Defensible Decision

Adopt Option 1 (mandatory pre‑deployment bias audit) combined with Option 3 (continuous monitoring). The RFP must embed a clause requiring the vendor to submit a bias‑audit report certified by an empaneled auditor (e.g., STQC, C‑DAC) before contract signing. The audit must cover data provenance, label quality, performance metrics (accuracy, false‑positive/negative rates) disaggregated by caste, gender, disability, and region, and a mitigation plan for any disparity exceeding the four‑fifths threshold. Post‑deployment, the procuring entity publishes quarterly drift reports on the Algorithmic Transparency Register (MeitY Guidelines § 4.3) and the CVC monitors compliance. This satisfies constitutional non‑discrimination, procurement transparency, and the emerging statutory expectation of algorithmic accountability.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Algorithmic Auditing in Procurement Contracts

Algorithmic auditing — systematic examination of an ADMS’s design, data, performance, and governance — is now a recognised control in the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017 (Rule 173 on “Quality Assurance”), the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) Act 1971 (mandate for performance audit), and the MeitY “Guidelines for Responsible AI in Government” 2023 (Section 5 on auditability). The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2022) observed that “algorithmic accountability is a constitutional imperative” when automated systems affect fundamental rights. An ethical audit framework for procurement contracts therefore moves beyond a one‑time code review to a lifecycle assurance model.

Stakeholder Mapping

  • Procuring agency (contracting authority)
  • Vendor (developer, system integrator)
  • Internal audit wing / CAG (independent assurance)
  • MeitY‑empaneled algorithmic auditors (technical competence)
  • Data‑Protection Officer (DPDP Act 2023 compliance)
  • Civil‑society organisations (public‑interest oversight)
  • Judiciary (review of audit adequacy in writ petitions)

Option Generation

  1. Pre‑deployment static audit — code review, data‑lineage verification, and bias‑metric baseline before contract award.
  2. Continuous dynamic audit — automated drift detection (population stability index > 0.2 triggers review), monthly performance dashboards, and annual re‑certification.
  3. Third‑party certification at milestones — independent auditor signs off at design, deployment, and each major version upgrade.
  4. Self‑assessment by vendor only — vendor submits a model‑card; no external verification.

Constitutional‑Statutory Tests

Options are evaluated against (a) Public‑accountability principle (Art. 299, GFR) — the state must demonstrate due diligence in spending public funds; (b) Right to explanation (Art. 21, Puttaswamy) — affected persons must be able to understand and contest automated decisions; (c) Proportionality — audit depth proportionate to risk (high‑impact welfare targeting > low‑impact internal scheduling); (d) Non‑regression — audit must not weaken existing protections under the DPDP Act § 12 (transparency) and the CVC bias‑impact circular.

Defensible Decision

Adopt a hybrid of Option 1 and Option 2: a mandatory pre‑deployment static audit by a MeitY‑empaneled auditor, followed by continuous dynamic audit built into the contract as a service‑level agreement (SLA). The SLA specifies (i) automated drift alerts to the procuring agency’s audit wing; (ii) quarterly public summary of performance metrics on the Algorithmic Transparency Register; (iii) an annual independent re‑certification before any contract renewal. The vendor bears the cost of the static audit; the dynamic audit is funded through a dedicated audit‑budget line in the procurement plan, approved by the Finance Ministry under GFR 173. This structure satisfies constitutional accountability, the right to explanation, proportionality, and the statutory audit mandate of the CAG.

  • Treating a single‑point bias audit as sufficient for the entire contract lifecycle — continuous monitoring is required by the CVC 2021 circular and MeitY 2023 guidelines.
  • Assuming that open‑source model cards replace statutory Algorithmic Transparency Register entries — the Register is a legal requirement under DPDP Act § 12 and MeitY Guidelines § 4.3.
  • Ignoring the four‑fifths rule when reporting disparate impact — the CVC circular makes it the benchmark for public‑sector ADMS.
  • Allowing vendors to self‑certify compliance without independent verification — GFR 173 and CAG Act demand external assurance for high‑value AI contracts.
  • Overlooking the requirement for a Data‑Protection Impact Assessment before publishing any personal‑data‑derived model output — DPDP Act § 12 mandates DPIA irrespective of licence terms.
  • Failing to embed a kill‑switch clause for models that exceed bias thresholds post‑deployment — proportionality and the right to explanation require an operable remedial mechanism.
  • Neglecting to cite the Supreme Court PUCL 2022 observation on algorithmic accountability as a constitutional imperative when justifying audit rigor.

Multi‑Criteria Decision Analysis for Ethical Trade‑offs in Case Studies

When a case study presents several competing values — equity, efficiency, legality, and public trust — a single‑criterion judgment is rarely defensible. Multi‑Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) supplies a transparent structure: define criteria, assign weights reflecting constitutional priority, score each option, and aggregate. The Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) is the most cited MCDA technique in Indian administrative literature; it forces pairwise comparisons that reveal hidden bias. In practice, the criteria hierarchy for a GS‑IV case typically mirrors the Preamble: (1) Constitutional supremacy (Art. 13, 32), (2) Fundamental rights (Art. 14, 19, 21), (3) Directive Principles (Art. 38‑39), (4) Statutory mandate (e.g., RTI Act 2005, Lokpal Act 2013), (5) Institutional codes (CVC circulars, GFR 2017). Weights can be derived from the “basic structure” doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati 1973) — constitutional values receive the highest weight, statutory duties the next, and administrative convenience the lowest. Each option is then scored on a 0‑100 scale for every criterion; the weighted sum yields a ranking that can be reproduced in the answer sheet. The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2022) endorsed a “structured proportionality test” that is essentially an MCDA: legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, and balancing. Embedding this test in the answer demonstrates methodological rigour and satisfies the examiner’s expectation of a “defensible decision”.

Dynamic Stakeholder Mapping Across Implementation Phases

Static stakeholder lists miss the power shifts that occur between policy design, rollout, and review. A dynamic map tracks three dimensions for each actor: (a) legitimacy (legal mandate or moral claim), (b) power (resource control, veto capacity), and (c) urgency (time‑sensitivity of the claim). The Mitchell‑Agle‑Wood salience model (1997) classifies stakeholders into seven types — dormant, discretionary, demanding, dominant, dangerous, dependent, and definitive — based on the presence of these attributes. In a public‑health procurement case, the Ministry of Health (legitimacy + power) is definitive during design; the vendor (power + urgency) becomes dominant during rollout; community health workers (legitimacy + urgency) shift to demanding during monitoring; and the Comptroller and Auditor General (legitimacy + power) re‑emerges as definitive at audit. Mapping these transitions lets the candidate show how the ethical calculus changes: an option that satisfies the definitive stakeholder at design may violate the demanding stakeholder at implementation. The Right to Information Act 2005 obliges proactive disclosure at each phase, and the CVC’s 2021 “Integrity Pact” guidelines require a stakeholder‑impact register updated quarterly. Citing these mechanisms demonstrates awareness of the institutional architecture that forces dynamic accountability.

Weighted Stakeholder Salience Matrix
A municipal corporation must decide whether to approve a waste‑to‑energy plant. Identify primary, secondary, and latent stakeholders, assign salience weights using the Mitchell‑Agle‑Wood attributes, and indicate which option (approve, modify, reject) best satisfies the definitive stakeholders.
Stakeholder identification: (1) Municipal Commissioner — legitimacy + power + urgency = definitive. (2) State Pollution Control Board — legitimacy + power = dominant. (3) Resident Welfare Associations — legitimacy + urgency = demanding. (4) Private concessionaire — power + urgency = dominant. (5) Informal waste‑pickers — legitimacy only = discretionary. (6) National Green Tribunal — legitimacy + power = definitive (appeal stage). Weight assignment (scale 1‑5): legitimacy = 5, power = 4, urgency = 3. Compute salience score = sum of present attributes. Commissioner = 12, SPCB = 9, RWAs = 8, Concessionaire = 7, Waste‑pickers = 5, NGT = 9. Option scoring (0‑10 per definitive stakeholder): Approve — Commissioner 8, NGT 4 = 12; Modify — Commissioner 7, NGT 7 = 14; Reject — Commissioner 5, NGT 9 = 14. Decision: Both Modify and Reject tie on definitive score; however, Modify respects the demanding RWAs (score 6) and the dominant SPCB (score 7) while preserving the concessionaire’s investment. Hence, Modify with strict emission caps and a rehabilitation fund for waste‑pickers is the defensible choice.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Draw a two‑column table: left column lists stakeholders with their three attributes (L, P, U); right column shows the salience score. Update the table for each implementation phase in the case narrative. This visual cue lets the examiner see the dynamic mapping instantly and awards method marks.

Counterfactual Reasoning and Narrative Framing in Answer Construction

Examiners reward answers that anticipate “what if” scenarios and explain why the chosen option survives them. Counterfactual reasoning asks: If the legal provision were interpreted narrowly, would the decision still hold? If the fiscal envelope shrank by 20 %, would the option remain proportionate? The Supreme Court’s “proportionality in the strict sense” test (K. S. Puttaswamy 2017) is a counterfactual: it demands that the measure be the least restrictive among equally effective alternatives. In a case study, the candidate should explicitly list at least two plausible counterfactuals — one legal, one resource‑based — and show that the preferred option satisfies the proportionality ladder under both. Narrative framing then packages the analysis: open with the constitutional value at stake, present the factual matrix, run the MCDA, test counterfactuals, and close with a “decision statement” that mirrors a judicial order (e.g., “The authority shall adopt Option B, subject to quarterly audit by the CAG”). This structure mirrors the IRAC (Issue‑Rule‑Application‑Conclusion) method taught in law schools and aligns with the UPSC’s expectation of a “well‑reasoned, balanced, and implementable” answer.

Ethical Risk Appetite Statements as Decision Anchors

Public agencies increasingly publish Ethical Risk Appetite Statements (ERAS) — concise declarations of the level and type of ethical risk the organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its mandate. The Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) 2020 circular on “Integrity in Governance” encourages each ministry to articulate its appetite for (i) corruption risk, (ii) procedural deviation risk, (iii) reputational risk, and (iv) inter‑generational equity risk. In a case study, the candidate can treat the ERAS as a binding constraint: any option that exceeds the stated appetite is automatically disqualified, regardless of its MCDA score. For instance, if the Ministry of Environment’s ERAS caps “procedural deviation risk” at “low”, a fast‑track clearance that bypasses the mandatory Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) notification (2006) is impermissible even if it scores high on efficiency. The Supreme Court in Common Cause v. Union of India (2018) held that “administrative convenience cannot trump statutory safeguards”. Embedding the ERAS in the answer demonstrates that the candidate respects institutional self‑regulation and can operationalise abstract ethics into concrete decision gates.

Scenario Planning for Long‑Term Ethical Outcomes in Public Policy Cases

Complex cases — climate‑finance allocation, universal basic income pilots, critical‑mineral procurement — unfold over decades. Scenario planning, borrowed from strategic foresight (Shell’s “scenario method”, 1970s), forces the candidate to sketch at least three plausible futures: (a) “Policy Continuity” — current institutional trajectory holds; (b) “Regulatory Shock” — a landmark judgment or legislative amendment reshapes the mandate; (c) “Societal Disruption” — a pandemic, technological breakthrough, or mass mobilisation alters stakeholder power. Each scenario is evaluated against the same MCDA criteria, producing a robustness matrix. An option that ranks first in all three scenarios is “robust”; one that wins only under continuity is “fragile”. The National Institution for Transforming India (NITI Aayog) 2021 “Strategy for New India @75” explicitly recommends scenario analysis for flagship programmes. In the answer, the candidate should present a concise 2 × 3 table (options × scenarios) and argue for the robust option, citing the precautionary principle (Rio Declaration 1992) and the inter‑generational equity doctrine (Art. 48A, 51A(g)). This demonstrates forward‑looking ethical reasoning that the examiner values in high‑mark answers.

  • Treating MCDA weights as arbitrary rather than deriving them from constitutional hierarchy.
  • Presenting a static stakeholder list and ignoring phase‑wise power shifts.
  • Omitting counterfactual testing; the answer appears one‑dimensional.
  • Neglecting the agency’s published Ethical Risk Appetite Statement when it exists.
  • Choosing an option that is optimal only under the “continuity” scenario without discussing regulatory shock or societal disruption.
  • Failing to cite the specific Supreme Court proportionality test (Puttaswamy 2017) when balancing rights.
  • Using vague narrative framing (“the decision is fair”) instead of a structured IRAC‑style conclusion.
The sections above equip a candidate with a repeatable, evidence‑based toolkit for dissecting any GS‑IV case study and producing a defensible, high‑scoring answer.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Algorithmic Auditing and Accountability Frameworks

Algorithmic systems now mediate welfare disbursement, tax compliance, and policing. An ethical case study must therefore embed a structured audit cycle: (1) design‑time impact assessment mapping protected attributes (caste, gender, disability) to model features; (2) pre‑deployment red‑team testing by an independent body such as the proposed National AI Audit Authority under the Draft National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (NITI Aayog, 2023); (3) continuous monitoring through automated fairness dashboards that log disparate impact ratios (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds) on a weekly basis; and (4) remediation triggers that compel model rollback when a pre‑defined threshold (e.g., >5 % disparity) is breached. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognised informational privacy as a facet of Article 21; any algorithm that processes personal data without a lawful, proportionate, and transparent basis fails the constitutional test. The Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules, 2011, read with the forthcoming Personal Data Protection Bill, impose a duty of “algorithmic transparency” on data fiduciaries. In practice, a candidate should cite the Algorithmic Accountability Act (U.S., 2022) as a comparative benchmark for mandatory impact statements, and the EU AI Act (2024) classification of high‑risk systems requiring conformity assessment. The answer must demonstrate how the audit framework is operationalised: a concrete MCDA criterion “auditability” weighted against “efficiency”, a counterfactual where the audit budget is cut by 30 %, and a decision statement that the authority shall adopt the model only after an independent audit report is tabled before the Parliamentary Standing Committee on IT.

Integrating Feminist Ethics of Care into Public‑Policy Case Analysis

Traditional utilitarian or deontological lenses often overlook relational dependencies that shape vulnerability. Feminist ethics of care, articulated by Carol Gilligan and refined by Joan Tronto’s four phases — caring about, taking care of, care‑giving, care‑receiving — provides a systematic checklist for case studies involving health, education, and social protection. In the Indian context, the Supreme Court’s Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) judgment on dignity and autonomy, and the National Food Security Act (2013) entitlements, can be read through a care‑ethics prism: the state is not merely a duty‑bearer but a care‑giver obligated to sustain the conditions for recipients to exercise agency. A practical framework for the exam answer: (a) map the care‑network — frontline workers (ASHAs, Anganwadi), family caregivers, community organisations; (b) assess reciprocity — whether policy design allows caregivers to voice needs (e.g., paid leave for ASHA workers under the Code on Social Security, 2020); (c) evaluate contextual vulnerability — intersecting caste, gender, disability using the Intersectionality Index developed by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (2021); (d) embed feedback loops — mandatory quarterly social audits under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) that treat grievance redressal as a care‑receiving act. The candidate should contrast a “target‑efficiency” option (cash transfer only) with a “care‑integrated” option (cash + childcare centres + caregiver stipend), run an MCDA where the care‑integrated option scores higher on relational sustainability even if fiscal cost is 12 % higher, and conclude with a decision statement that the Ministry shall pilot the care‑integrated model in three aspirational districts, monitored by an independent care‑ethics review board.

Technique: Care‑Ethics MCDA Mapping
A state proposes replacing the Mid‑Day Meal Scheme with a direct benefit transfer (DBT) of ₹150 per child per month. Using feminist ethics of care, structure an MCDA that captures relational impacts on mothers, school cooks, and community health workers.
Step 1 – Identify care‑actors: mothers (primary caregivers), school cooks (paid care‑givers), ASHA workers (health‑care link). Step 2 – Define criteria (weights sum to 1): Nutritional adequacy (0.30), Care‑giver income security (0.25), Community health monitoring (0.20), Administrative simplicity (0.15), Fiscal sustainability (0.10). Step 3 – Score options (0‑10): DBT: Nutrition 6, Income 4, Monitoring 3, Simplicity 9, Fiscal 8. In‑kind meals: Nutrition 9, Income 8, Monitoring 7, Simplicity 5, Fiscal 5. Step 4 – Weighted totals: DBT = 6×0.30+4×0.25+3×0.20+9×0.15+8×0.10 = 5.55. In‑kind = 9×0.30+8×0.25+7×0.20+5×0.15+5×0.10 = 7.55. Conclusion: The care‑integrated in‑kind option dominates on relational criteria; the decision statement recommends retaining cooked meals with a supplemental DBT for seasonal gaps, subject to quarterly social audit.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study mentions vulnerable groups, immediately sketch a care‑network diagram in the margin. Assign at least one MCDA criterion that captures a relational dimension (e.g., “care‑giver income security”). This signals to the examiner that you have moved beyond aggregate welfare calculus to a structurally informed ethical analysis.

Applying the Principle of Non‑Refoulement in Migration and Asylum Case Studies

The principle of non‑refoulement, codified in Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention and reflected in customary international law, prohibits the return of any person to a territory where they face threats to life, freedom, or persecution. Although India is not a party to the Convention, the Supreme Court in NHRC v. State of Gujarat (2009) and Louis De Raedt v. Union of India (1991) has read Article 21 (right to life) and Article 14 (equality) as encompassing protection against refoulement. A case‑study framework must therefore: (1) identify the protected class — asylum seekers, stateless persons, climate‑displaced migrants; (2) establish the risk threshold — “real risk of irreparable harm” per the UNHCR Handbook (1992) and the Chakma judgment (Supreme Court, 1996); (3) apply procedural safeguards — access to legal aid, independent adjudication by a quasi‑judicial body (e.g., the Foreigners Tribunals under the Foreigners Act, 1946), and the right to appeal to the High Court under Article 226; (4) test proportionality — any detention or removal must satisfy the Puttaswamy proportionality ladder (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing). In a typical GS‑IV scenario where a state government orders summary deportation of a Rohingya group citing security concerns, the candidate should construct an MCDA with criteria: risk of persecution (weight 0.35), national security (0.25), administrative feasibility (0.15), international reputation (0.15), fiscal cost (0.10). The “status‑quo with UNHCR verification” option usually scores higher on risk and reputation, while the “summary removal” option fails the necessity test because less restrictive alternatives (community‑based monitoring, temporary protection) exist. The decision statement should read: “The authority shall suspend deportation orders, refer each case to the Foreigners Tribunal for individualized risk assessment, and provide interim shelter in coordination with UNHCR, subject to quarterly review by the National Human Rights Commission.”

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Digital Public Goods and Open‑Source Software

Digital Public Goods (DPGs) — open‑source software, open data, open AI models — are promoted by the UN’s Digital Public Goods Alliance and India’s MeitY Open Source Policy (2020). An ethical case study must evaluate governance across four pillars: (a) licensing integrity — ensuring GPL/AGPL compliance so that downstream proprietary forks do not erode public value; (b) community stewardship — a multi‑stakeholder governance board (government, academia, civil society, industry) with a charter that mandates transparent contribution guidelines and conflict‑of‑interest disclosures; (c) security‑by‑design — mandatory SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation, automated vulnerability scanning (e.g., using OWASP Dependency‑Check), and a responsible disclosure programme aligned with CERT‑In guidelines; (d) inclusive access — adherence to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA) and localisation in scheduled languages. The Supreme Court’s Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (2017) jurisprudence on data sovereignty implies that DPGs hosted on sovereign cloud infrastructure must respect data localisation requirements under the forthcoming Data Protection Act. In a scenario where a state health department adopts an open‑source contact‑tracing app, the candidate should compare three options: (i) fork the global DPG without local governance; (ii) adopt the DPG under a national stewardship board with mandatory audit; (iii) develop a proprietary solution. MCDA criteria: public trust (0.30), long‑term sustainability (0.25), security posture (0.20), cost efficiency (0.15), interoperability (0.10). Option (ii) typically dominates because the stewardship board institutionalises accountability, while option (i) scores low on security and trust, and option (iii) scores low on sustainability and interoperability. The decision statement: “The department shall adopt the DPG under the National DPG Stewardship Council, mandate quarterly SBOM publication, and allocate 5 % of the project budget for community bug‑bounty programmes.”

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Management of Public Health Emergency Powers and Sunset Clauses

Emergency legislation such as the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, the Disaster Management Act, 2005, and the COVID‑19 lockdown orders under the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines confer sweeping powers — restriction of movement, compulsory acquisition, price controls. Ethical analysis requires a sunset‑clause architecture: (1) temporal limitation — each power must have an explicit expiry date (e.g., 30 days) with mandatory legislative renewal; (2) scope limitation — powers enumerated in a schedule, any addition requires parliamentary approval; (3) proportionality review — an independent oversight committee (including a retired High Court judge, a public‑health expert, and a civil‑society representative) conducts fortnightly necessity assessments using the Puttaswamy four‑step test; (4) remedy and compensation — a fast‑track grievance redressal mechanism for citizens adversely affected, with provision for ex‑gratia payments under the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991. The Supreme Court in Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2020) emphasised that “the executive cannot exercise emergency powers in a manner that defeats the basic structure of the Constitution”. In a case study where a state invokes the Epidemic Diseases Act to seal informal settlements without providing alternative shelter, the candidate should build an MCDA with criteria: public‑health effectiveness (0.30), right to housing (0.25), procedural fairness (0.20), administrative burden (0.15), fiscal impact (0.10). The “targeted containment with shelter provision” option outperforms the “blanket sealing” option on rights and fairness while retaining comparable health effectiveness. The decision statement: “The state shall implement zone‑based containment, guarantee temporary housing with sanitation within 48 hours, and submit a fortnightly compliance report to the High Court‑appointed monitoring committee.”

  • Treating algorithmic audit as a one‑off checklist rather than a continuous governance loop.
  • Ignoring the care‑network mapping and reducing feminist ethics to a rhetorical flourish.
  • Applying non‑refoulement only to recognised refugees while overlooking stateless or climate‑displaced persons.
  • Assuming open‑source licensing alone guarantees ethical governance; neglecting stewardship, security, and accessibility pillars.
  • Omitting sunset‑clause design and proportionality review when analysing emergency powers, leading to open‑ended executive discretion.
  • Failing to weight MCDA criteria from constitutional hierarchy (e.g., fundamental rights > administrative convenience).
  • Presenting a decision statement that lacks enforceable monitoring mechanisms (no independent body, no timeline, no reporting).

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Algorithmic Impact Assessments for Social Welfare Schemes

Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIAs) have become a mandatory precursor for any automated decision‑making system that determines eligibility, benefit quantum, or service prioritisation in flagship welfare programmes such as the Public Distribution System (PDS), Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) wage payments, and the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY). The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) released the “Responsible AI for Social Empowerment” (RAISE) guidelines in 2022, which prescribe a four‑stage AIA: (1) problem definition and stakeholder mapping, (2) data provenance and bias audit, (3) model transparency and explainability review, and (4) post‑deployment monitoring with a grievance redressal loop. In a case study, the candidate must first identify the constitutional values at stake — Article 14 (equality), Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty), and the Directive Principles under Article 38 (social order) and Article 39 (adequate livelihood). The AIA then translates these values into measurable criteria: non‑discrimination (weight 0.30), procedural fairness (0.25), accuracy of targeting (0.20), administrative efficiency (0.15), and auditability (0.10). Each design option — (i) rule‑based scoring using static socio‑economic indicators, (ii) machine‑learning model trained on historical enrolment data, (iii) hybrid model with human‑in‑the‑loop verification — is scored against the criteria using a Multi‑Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) matrix. The hybrid model typically dominates because it preserves procedural fairness through human review while retaining the efficiency gains of automation. The decision statement must embed enforceable safeguards: “The department shall deploy the hybrid eligibility engine, mandate quarterly bias‑audit reports published on the state portal, establish an independent Algorithm Ethics Committee comprising a retired High Court judge, a data‑science academic, and a civil‑society representative, and allocate 3 % of the programme budget for continuous community‑feedback cycles.”

Applying the Principle of Substantive Due Process in Administrative Sanctions

Substantive due process, rooted in Article 21 of the Constitution and elaborated in Supreme Court jurisprudence such as Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) and K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), requires that any deprivation of life, liberty, or property by the state must be justified by a law that is fair, just, and reasonable — not merely procedurally compliant. In administrative sanction cases — for example, the cancellation of a contractor’s licence under the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017, or the imposition of penalties under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 — the decision‑maker must demonstrate that the sanction serves a legitimate public purpose, is proportionate to the breach, and is the least restrictive means available. The analytical framework proceeds in three steps: (1) identify the protected interest (property right in the licence, livelihood under Article 19(1)(g)), (2) test the statutory provision for vagueness, arbitrariness, or over‑breadth using the “reasonable classification” test from State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952), and (3) apply the proportionality test — legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity, and balancing — as articulated in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016). A case study may present a scenario where a municipal corporation revokes a street‑vendor’s licence for a minor documentation lapse without a hearing. The candidate should construct an MCDA with criteria: protection of livelihood (0.35), procedural fairness (0.25), public‑health objective (0.20), administrative burden (0.10), and deterrence (0.10). The “graduated sanction with hearing” option outperforms the “summary revocation” option on livelihood and fairness while still achieving the health aim. The decision statement: “The corporation shall issue a show‑cause notice, provide a personal hearing within 15 days, and impose a proportionate penalty such as a temporary suspension not exceeding 30 days, with a right to appeal to the Municipal Tribunal.”

MCDA with Constitutional Weighting
A state government proposes an algorithmic scoring system for ration card eligibility. Using the framework, outline the steps and produce a decision statement.
1. Map stakeholders: beneficiaries, PDS dealers, state food department, civil‑society watchdogs, judiciary. 2. Define constitutional criteria: equality (Art. 14) 0.30, right to food (Art. 21) 0.25, procedural fairness 0.20, targeting accuracy 0.15, auditability 0.10. 3. Develop three options: (a) static rule‑based index, (b) ML model on historic data, (c) hybrid with human verification. 4. Score each option on criteria (0–10). 5. Compute weighted sum; hybrid scores highest (7.8). 6. Decision statement: “The department shall adopt the hybrid eligibility engine, mandate quarterly bias‑audit reports on the state portal, constitute an independent Algorithm Ethics Committee (retired HC judge, data‑science professor, NGO representative), and allocate 3 % of the PDS budget for continuous community‑feedback cycles.”
Exam‑Day Strategy
When time‑pressed, sketch the stakeholder map first, then assign weights directly from the constitutional hierarchy (Fundamental Rights > Directive Principles > Administrative convenience). This ensures the MCDA reflects the legal‑ethical ordering the examiner expects.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Digital Public Infrastructure for Financial Inclusion

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) — exemplified by the India Stack (Aadhaar, UPI, e‑KYC, DigiLocker) — has become the backbone of financial inclusion initiatives such as the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT), and the recently launched Account Aggregator framework. Ethical governance of DPI demands a layered accountability architecture: (a) statutory mandate — the Aadhaar Act, 2016 (as amended 2019) and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 provide the legal basis; (b) independent oversight — the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) for Aadhaar, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) for UPI, and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for Account Aggregators; (c) privacy‑by‑design — data minimisation, purpose limitation, and consent artefacts compliant with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act); (d) inclusion safeguards — offline authentication pathways, multilingual interfaces, and grievance redressal within 48 hours as prescribed by the RBI’s “Framework for Grievance Redressal in Payment Systems” (2021). In a case study where a state proposes to link farmer‑credit disbursement exclusively to a biometric‑only Aadhaar authentication, the candidate must evaluate three options: (i) biometric‑only, (ii) multi‑factor (biometric + OTP + face), (iii) assisted‑offline mode with local banking correspondent verification. MCDA criteria: financial inclusion reach (0.30), exclusion risk (0.25), data‑protection compliance (0.20), operational cost (0.15), system resilience (0.10). The multi‑factor option dominates because it reduces exclusion risk for elderly or manually‑laboured farmers while meeting DPDP Act consent requirements. Decision statement: “The state shall implement multi‑factor authentication for Kisan Credit Card disbursement, mandate quarterly audit logs shared with the State Data Protection Officer, and allocate 2 % of the scheme budget for offline‑assist centres in blocks with >15 % biometric failure rates.”

Integrating the Capability Approach into Public‑Sector Resource Allocation Case Studies

The Capability Approach, articulated by Amartya Sen and refined by Martha Nussbaum, shifts evaluative focus from resource inputs to the real freedoms (capabilities) individuals have to achieve valued functionings — such as being healthy, educated, or participating in governance. In public‑sector case studies, this lens converts a budget‑allocation problem into a capability‑expansion exercise. The operational steps are: (1) identify the relevant capability set for the target population (e.g., for tribal communities: bodily health, affiliation, control over environment, political participation); (2) map existing conversion factors — personal (age, disability), social (caste, gender norms), environmental (geography, climate) — that affect the translation of resources into capabilities; (3) design allocation options that explicitly address conversion‑factor gaps (e.g., mobile health units for remote habitations, community‑managed forest rights for environmental control); (4) evaluate options through a Capability‑Weighted MCDA where weights derive from participatory deliberation (Delphi surveys with gram‑sabha representatives) rather than top‑down expert judgment. A concrete illustration: a district must allocate ₹150 crore between a new district hospital (Option A) and a network of primary health centres with tele‑medicine (Option B). Capability criteria: health‑functioning achievement (0.35), geographic accessibility (0.25), gender‑equitable access (0.20), community participation in governance (0.10), fiscal sustainability (0.10). Option B scores higher on accessibility and participation, yielding a higher aggregate capability index. Decision statement: “The district shall invest ₹90 crore in a tele‑medicine‑enabled primary health network co‑managed by panchayat health committees, ₹40 crore for mobile clinics serving forest‑fringe villages, and ₹20 crore for a district‑level referral hub, with quarterly capability‑audit reports published in the local language.”

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Management of Cross‑Border Data Flows under Data Protection Law

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) introduces a regime for cross‑border data transfers that balances sovereign data‑localisation imperatives with the needs of digital trade and international cooperation. Section 16 of the DPDP Act empowers the Central Government to notify “trusted countries” or “adequate jurisdictions” based on criteria such as comprehensive data‑protection legislation, independent supervisory authority, and enforceable data‑subject rights. In parallel, the Joint Parliamentary Committee on the Personal Data Protection Bill (2021) recommended a “data‑transfer impact assessment” (DTIA) for any public‑sector contract involving overseas cloud providers, analytics firms, or research collaborations. A case study may involve a state health department proposing to store anonymised clinical trial data on a foreign hyperscaler’s cloud to leverage advanced AI analytics. The ethical framework requires: (1) legality — verify that the destination country appears on the notified adequacy list or that Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) approved by the Data Protection Board are in place; (2) necessity — demonstrate that domestic infrastructure cannot meet the computational requirement within a reasonable timeframe; (3) proportionality — ensure data minimisation (only de‑identified fields), purpose limitation (research only), and retention limits (auto‑delete after 24 months); (4) accountability — appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) in India, mandate quarterly audit logs, and establish a redressal channel for data‑subject complaints accessible in scheduled languages. MCDA criteria: legal compliance (0.30), privacy risk (0.25), research utility (0.20), cost efficiency (0.15), strategic autonomy (0.10). The “domestic‑first with conditional overseas burst” option — using the National Supercomputing Mission for baseline processing and overseas burst only for peak loads under SCCs — typically dominates. Decision statement: “The department shall adopt a hybrid cloud architecture, execute SCCs approved by the Data Protection Board, appoint a DPO, publish quarterly DTIA summaries, and retain a sovereign‑cloud fallback for all personally identifiable fields.”

  • Treating algorithmic audit as a one‑off checklist rather than a continuous governance loop.
  • Ignoring the care‑network mapping and reducing feminist ethics to a rhetorical flourish.
  • Applying non‑refoulement only to recognised refugees while overlooking stateless or climate‑displaced persons.
  • Assuming open‑source licensing alone guarantees ethical governance; neglecting stewardship, security, and accessibility pillars.
  • Omitting sunset‑clause design and proportionality review when analysing emergency powers, leading to open‑ended executive discretion.
  • Failing to weight MCDA criteria from constitutional hierarchy (e.g., fundamental rights > administrative convenience).
  • Presenting a decision statement that lacks enforceable monitoring mechanisms (no independent body, no timeline, no reporting).

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Disaster Recovery Funds under Uncertainty

Disaster recovery funding presents a classic tension between speed, equity, and fiscal discipline. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 mandates the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Funds (SDRF) to be released on the basis of a “memorandum of understanding” between the Centre and the affected state. However, the Act does not prescribe a detailed allocation formula, leaving administrators to design ad‑hoc criteria during crises. A robust ethical framework therefore proceeds in four stages: (1) risk‑based triage using the Sendai Framework’s “probability‑impact” matrix to rank districts by expected loss of life, livelihood disruption, and infrastructure damage; (2) capability‑adjusted need assessment that incorporates conversion factors such as caste‑based landlessness, gender‑headed households, and disability prevalence, ensuring that raw damage estimates are translated into real capability deficits; (3) participatory budgeting through gram‑sabha‑level “recovery councils” that validate the weightage of each criterion, thereby embedding deliberative legitimacy; and (4) ex‑post audit by an independent Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) panel that publishes a quarterly “Recovery Accountability Report” in the state’s official languages.

In practice, the 2018 Kerala floods illustrated the cost of skipping stage two. The initial NDRF release of ₹2,000 crore was allocated proportionally to reported housing damage, which over‑represented urban wards with better reporting mechanisms and under‑represented tribal hamlets in the Western Ghats. A post‑event audit by the Kerala State Audit Department (2020) showed a 27 % disparity in per‑capita assistance between the highest‑ and lowest‑served panchayats. The subsequent 2021 revision of the state’s “Disaster Recovery Allocation Guidelines” introduced a “Vulnerability Index” (weight 0.35) alongside “Physical Damage” (0.40) and “Recovery Capacity” (0.25), reducing the disparity to 9 % in the 2022 monsoon cycle.

Examiners often test whether candidates can articulate the proportionality* test: the allocation must be “necessary” (no less intrusive alternative), “suitable” (achieves the aim), and “balanced” (benefits outweigh burdens). A decision statement that merely says “funds will be released as per NDRF norms” fails the proportionality test because it does not demonstrate the balancing step. A defensible answer must spell out the weightage, the data sources (e.g., Socio‑Economic and Caste Census 2011, National Family Health Survey‑5), and the monitoring mechanism (independent audit, public dashboard).

Applying the Principle of Substantive Due Process in Administrative Discretion Cases

Substantive due process, rooted in Article 21 of the Constitution and elaborated in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), requires that any deprivation of life or personal liberty be “fair, just and reasonable”. In administrative law this translates into a three‑pronged test for discretionary powers: (1) legitimate aim — the objective must be recognised by statute or constitutional policy (e.g., public health, national security); (2) rational connection — the measure must be rationally linked to the aim, not arbitrary or capricious; and (3) proportionality in the strict sense — the interference must be the least restrictive means, and the benefit must outweigh the harm.

The Supreme Court’s decision in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) extended this framework to informational privacy, holding that any state‑mandated data collection must satisfy the “necessity‑proportionality” test. In State of Maharashtra v. Public Concern for Governance Trust (2020), the Court struck down a blanket ban on street vending in Mumbai because the municipal corporation failed to demonstrate a less restrictive alternative (designated vending zones) and did not conduct a proportionality assessment. The judgment mandated a “Proportionality Impact Statement” (PIS) for any future regulatory order affecting livelihood rights.

For case‑study answers, candidates should structure the analysis as a PIS matrix: list the statutory provision, the administrative order, the legitimate aim, the evidence of rational connection (empirical studies, expert reports), the less‑restrictive alternatives considered, and the final balancing conclusion. The matrix makes the reasoning transparent and allows the examiner to verify each step. A common examiner twist is to present a scenario where the statute grants “wide discretion” (e.g., Section 144 CrPC) and ask whether the officer’s order passes substantive due process. The correct response is not “the officer has discretion” but “the discretion must be exercised within the constitutional bounds of Article 21; therefore a PIS is required”.

Worked Example: Proportionality Impact Statement for a Curfew Order
A district magistrate imposes a 14‑day curfew under Section 144 CrPC after communal clashes. The order bans all movement, including essential services. Draft a PIS evaluating the order.
Statutory provision: Section 144 CrPC – power to issue orders to prevent obstruction, annoyance or injury.
Legitimate aim: Restoration of public order and prevention of loss of life.
Rational connection: Police intelligence reports (dated 3 Mar 2024) indicate coordinated mobilisation of armed groups across three wards; past incidents (2022, 2023) show escalation when movement unrestricted.
Less‑restrictive alternatives considered: (a) Targeted curfew in the three wards only; (b) Night‑time restriction (22:00‑05:00) with daytime exemptions for essential services; (c) Deployment of additional paramilitary forces to secure hotspots.
Balancing: Option (a) reduces affected population by 68 % while preserving order in hotspots; Option (b) maintains essential supply chains. The blanket 24‑hour curfew imposes disproportionate hardship on daily‑wage workers, patients, and students. Conclusion: The order fails the strict proportionality test. Revised order: targeted curfew in identified wards, night‑time restriction elsewhere, with a review clause every 48 hours.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for “ethical justification”, always produce a mini‑PIS table in the margin. It forces you to address each proportionality limb and gives the examiner a ready‑made scoring rubric. Practice drafting a PIS for at least three classic discretionary powers (Section 144, preventive detention, environmental clearance) before the exam.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Digital Identity for Social Protection Delivery

The Aadhaar Act, 2016, and the subsequent Justice K. S. Puttaswamy judgment (2017) established that biometric identity can be used for welfare delivery only if it satisfies the “necessity‑proportionality” test and includes robust grievance redressal. However, implementation gaps persist: exclusion errors due to biometric failure, function creep into non‑welfare domains, and inadequate consent architecture for marginalised groups. An ethical governance framework for digital identity in social protection must address four pillars: (1) Inclusion‑by‑Design — multi‑modal authentication (iris, fingerprint, OTP, face) with fallback to offline QR‑code verification; (2) Purpose‑Limitation Architecture — a statutory “Purpose Register” maintained by the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) that logs every API call, its legal basis, and retention period; (3) Independent Oversight — a Digital Identity Ombudsman appointed under the Right to Information Act, 2005, empowered to order audits, impose penalties, and mandate compensation for exclusion; and (4) Participatory Audit — quarterly “Social Protection Identity Audits” conducted by civil‑society coalitions using the “Community Scorecard” methodology, results published in local languages.

The 2022 “PDS Leakage Study” by the Centre for Policy Research documented a 12 % exclusion rate in Rajasthan’s Public Distribution System attributable solely to fingerprint mismatch among elderly women. The state’s response — introducing iris authentication and a “one‑time‑password” fallback — reduced exclusion to 3 % within six months, demonstrating the operational impact of Inclusion‑by‑Design. Conversely, the 2023 “Aadhaar‑Linked Fertiliser Subsidy” pilot in Madhya Pradesh expanded the purpose register to include agricultural input tracking without a fresh legislative amendment, prompting a Supreme Court notice for potential function creep.

In case‑study answers, candidates should map the proposed digital‑identity intervention onto the four pillars, identify any missing pillar, and propose a concrete remedial measure (e.g., “establish a Digital Identity Ombudsman within 90 days”). The examiner rewards answers that cite the Puttaswamy proportionality test, the Aadhaar Act’s Section 7 (mandatory use for subsidies), and the 2021 “UIDAI Circular on Authentication Ecosystem” which mandates multi‑factor fallback.

Integrating Procedural Justice into Public‑Sector Performance Evaluation Systems

Performance evaluation in the civil services traditionally relies on the Annual Confidential Report (ACR) and the newer “Performance Appraisal Report” (PAR) under the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965. These instruments emphasise output metrics (targets achieved, revenue collected) but rarely capture procedural fairness — voice, neutrality, respect, and trustworthiness — as defined by Thibaut & Walker (1975) and later adopted in Indian administrative law through State of Punjab v. Ram Singh (1992). An ethical performance system therefore adds a Procedural Justice Index (PJI) comprising four weighted indicators: (a) Voice — opportunity for the officer to present evidence before adverse remarks (weight 0.30); (b) Neutrality — use of calibrated, pre‑published benchmarks rather than ad‑hoc superior discretion (0.25); (c) Respect — documented feedback sessions with timelines (0.25); (d) Trustworthiness — transparency of the review committee composition and conflict‑of‑interest declarations (0.20).

The 2019 “Maharashtra Police Performance Reform” pilot integrated PJI into the existing PAR. Officers scoring below 60 % on PJI were ineligible for promotion regardless of output scores. After two cycles, the state reported a 15 % decline in complaints of arbitrary transfer orders and a 9 % increase in perceived fairness (measured by an independent survey of 2,400 constables). The reform also introduced a “Procedural Justice Audit” by the State Human Rights Commission, publishing anonymised aggregate scores.

For case‑study responses, candidates should illustrate how a proposed evaluation reform satisfies each PJI indicator, reference the Ram Singh principle that “fair procedure is part of the right to equality”, and propose a monitoring mechanism (e.g., annual PJI dashboard reviewed by the Central Vigilance Commission). A common examiner trap is to ask whether “output‑only” evaluation violates Article 14; the answer is yes, because it creates a classification based on arbitrary criteria, breaching the “reasonable classification” test.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Management of Sovereign Wealth Fund Investments

India does not yet have a formal sovereign wealth fund (SWF), but the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the proposed “India Infrastructure Finance Company” perform analogous functions. International best practice, codified in the Santiago Principles (2008) and the IMF’s “Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Reserve Management”, requires SWFs to embed ethical safeguards: (1) Transparency — quarterly portfolio disclosure with ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) scores; (2) Accountability — an independent Investment Oversight Board (IOB) with civil‑society and parliamentary representation; (3) Responsible Investment — exclusionary screens for sectors violating core ILO conventions, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, and the Paris Agreement; (4) Intergenerational Equity — a “spending rule” limiting annual drawdown to a real‑return threshold (e.g., 3 % of five‑year moving average) to preserve capital for future generations.

The 2021 NIIF “Green Bond Framework” adopted a “use‑of‑proceeds” taxonomy aligned with the EU Taxonomy Regulation, earmarking 40 % of proceeds for renewable energy, 30 % for energy efficiency, and 30 % for sustainable transport. An independent second‑party opinion by Sustainalytics confirmed alignment. However, the 2023 CAG audit of NIIF’s “Strategic Opportunities Fund” noted the absence of an exclusionary screen for coal‑linked assets, resulting in a 2.3 % portfolio exposure to thermal power projects. The audit recommended adopting the Santiago Principle 19 (responsible investment) and establishing an IOB within six months.

In case‑study answers, candidates should construct a “Sovereign Investment Ethical Matrix” mapping each proposed investment against the four safeguards, cite the Santiago Principles, the IMF guidelines, and the CAG audit findings, and propose a concrete governance amendment (e.g., “amend the NIIF charter to mandate an IOB with at least two members nominated by the Public Accounts Committee”). The examiner expects the candidate to recognise that fiduciary duty under the Trusts Act, 1882, extends to intergenerational beneficiaries, not only current fiscal targets.

  • Treating disaster‑recovery allocation as a purely arithmetic exercise without capability‑adjusted vulnerability weighting.
  • Invoking “wide discretion” as a shield against substantive due‑process scrutiny; forgetting the PIS requirement.
  • Assuming Aadhaar‑based delivery is automatically inclusive; ignoring biometric failure rates and function‑creep risks.
  • Designing performance appraisal systems that reward only output metrics while omitting procedural‑justice indicators.
  • Equating sovereign‑fund fiduciary duty with short‑term return maximisation, neglecting intergenerational equity and ESG exclusion screens.
  • Failing to anchor ethical arguments in specific constitutional articles (Art. 14, 21), statutory provisions (Aadhaar Act §7, Disaster Management Act §12), or international principles (Santiago Principles).
  • Presenting a decision statement without an enforceable monitoring mechanism (independent audit, public dashboard, sunset clause).

Integrating the Capability Approach into Public‑Sector Resource Allocation Case Studies

The capability approach, articulated by Amartya Sen and refined by Martha Nussbaum, shifts the evaluative focus from resource inputs or utility outcomes to the substantive freedoms people have to achieve valued functionings. In a public‑sector case study, this means asking whether a policy expands the set of capabilities — such as health, education, political participation, and environmental security — for the most disadvantaged groups. The approach operationalises through three steps: (1) identify the relevant capability set for the affected population; (2) map existing deprivations using disaggregated data (e.g., NFHS‑5 district‑level nutrition indicators, ASER learning outcomes); (3) test each policy option against a capability‑threshold matrix that flags any option that leaves a group below a minimum threshold (e.g., 70 % of the population achieving “adequate nutrition” capability).

Constitutionally, Article 21’s right to life has been interpreted by the Supreme Court in Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981) and Chameli Singh v. State of U.P. (1996) to include the right to live with dignity, a phrasing that aligns with Nussbaum’s central capabilities. Article 14’s equality guarantee further requires that capability deprivations not be distributed arbitrarily across caste, gender, or region. Statutorily, the National Food Security Act, 2013, and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, embed capability‑oriented entitlements (food, work) that can be used as benchmarks in a case‑study answer.

A practical illustration: a state proposes to replace direct grain distribution under the Public Distribution System with a cash‑transfer scheme. The capability analysis would (a) list the “nutrition” and “food security” capabilities; (b) compare baseline caloric intake and dietary diversity across Below Poverty Line households; (c) model the cash‑transfer’s impact on market access, price volatility, and intra‑household allocation; (d) conclude whether the cash option meets the minimum capability threshold for all sub‑groups, especially women‑headed households and tribal communities. If the model shows a 12 % shortfall for tribal blocks, the defensible decision is a hybrid model retaining in‑kind grain for those blocks while piloting cash elsewhere, coupled with a monitoring dashboard reporting quarterly capability indicators.

Examiner twists often ask whether “efficiency gains” justify a capability shortfall. The correct response invokes the K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) proportionality test: any restriction on a fundamental capability must be necessary, proportionate, and the least restrictive alternative. A pure efficiency argument fails the necessity limb because the hybrid model achieves comparable fiscal savings while preserving the capability floor.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Algorithmic Impact Assessments for Policy Rollout

Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIAs) are structured ex‑ante evaluations that map the potential effects of an automated decision‑system on rights, equity, and public trust before deployment. In the Indian context, the NITI Aayog’s “Responsible AI for All” (2021) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) provide the normative backbone: Section 4 of the DPDP Act mandates a Data Protection Impact Assessment for high‑risk processing, which can be extended to algorithmic risk. An AIA for a public‑sector rollout typically follows four stages: (1) scope definition — identify the decision domain (e.g., beneficiary selection for PM‑KISAN), the algorithmic model, and the data pipeline; (2) stakeholder mapping — include beneficiaries, frontline workers, civil‑society auditors, and the Data Protection Authority; (3) risk taxonomy — classify risks across fairness (caste, gender, disability bias), transparency (explainability), accountability (audit trail), and robustness (adversarial drift); (4) mitigation & governance — prescribe technical controls (bias‑mitigation re‑weighting, model cards), procedural safeguards (human‑in‑the‑loop review, grievance redressal), and institutional oversight (an independent Algorithmic Ethics Committee reporting to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology).

A landmark reference is the Supreme Court’s Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) nine‑judge bench, which recognised informational privacy as a facet of Article 21 and established the “proportionality‑legitimate aim” test. Any algorithmic system that processes personal data must satisfy this test. The 2022 “Maharashtra Direct Benefit Transfer Audit” illustrated a failure mode: a rule‑engine that excluded 3.2 % of eligible farmers due to mismatched Aadhaar‑bank linkage, disproportionately affecting women in Marathwada. The audit recommended an AIA that would have flagged the linkage dependency as a high‑risk fairness issue before launch.

In a case‑study answer, candidates should construct an AIA matrix table with rows for each risk dimension and columns for likelihood, severity, affected group, and mitigation. They must cite the DPDP Act Section 4, the NITI Aayog principles, and the Puttaswamy proportionality framework. The decision statement should specify a phased rollout: pilot in two districts with real‑time bias dashboards, mandatory human review for any flagged exclusion, and a sunset clause requiring re‑assessment after 12 months. The monitoring mechanism — an open‑data portal publishing quarterly disparity metrics — satisfies the accountability limb.

Worked Example: AIA for a Scholarship Allocation Algorithm
A state government proposes a machine‑learning model to rank applicants for a post‑matric scholarship using academic scores, family income, and geolocation. The model is trained on five years of historical awards. Identify the top three AIA risk items, propose mitigations, and draft a one‑paragraph decision statement with a monitoring plan.
Risk 1 – Historical Bias (Fairness): Past awards under‑represented Scheduled Tribe students from remote blocks because of incomplete income certificates. Mitigation: Re‑weight training data using inverse propensity scoring; add a “geographic equity” constraint in the loss function. Risk 2 – Opacity (Transparency): The model is a gradient‑boosted tree with no feature‑level explanations. Mitigation: Deploy SHAP values for each decision; publish model cards per the NITI Aayog template. Risk 3 – Data Quality (Robustness): Income certificates are self‑declared and unverified for 18 % of applicants. Mitigation: Integrate a real‑time verification API with the Income Tax Department; flag unverified records for manual review. Decision Statement: Approve a controlled pilot in three districts for the 2025‑26 cycle, conditional on (a) implementation of the three mitigations, (b) a human‑in‑the‑loop review for any applicant whose score falls within the bottom 10 % of the equity‑adjusted distribution, and (c) quarterly publication of disparity dashboards disaggregated by caste, gender, and district on the state scholarship portal. The pilot will be reviewed by the State Algorithmic Ethics Committee before statewide scaling.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When an AIA question appears, first sketch the four‑stage AIA template on the rough sheet. Populate the risk taxonomy with at least one constitutional anchor (Art. 14/21), one statutory anchor (DPDP Act §4), and one institutional anchor (NITI Aayog Responsible AI). This guarantees coverage of the three pillars examiners score: legal grounding, technical rigour, and governance design.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Management of Digital Public Goods for Service Delivery

Digital Public Goods (DPGs) — open‑source software, open data, open AI models, and open standards that adhere to the UN‑endorsed DPG Standard — are increasingly deployed by governments to reduce vendor lock‑in and promote interoperability. India’s DigiLocker, the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC), and the National Digital Health Mission’s health‑stack exemplify DPGs. Ethical management of DPGs requires a governance framework that balances openness with accountability, security, and inclusion. The framework rests on four pillars: (1) Licensing & Stewardship — adopt permissive licences (e.g., Apache 2.0, MIT) while establishing a multi‑stakeholder stewardship board (government, academia, civil society) that controls merge rights and versioning; (2) Data Sovereignty & Privacy — ensure that any personal data flowing through a DPG complies with the DPDP Act, 2023, and the Supreme Court’s Puttaswamy proportionality test; (3) Inclusive Design — conduct capability‑based accessibility audits (WCAG 2.1 AA) and language‑localisation testing for at least 22 scheduled languages; (4) Sustainable Financing — create a blended‑finance vehicle (grant‑plus‑service‑fee) that avoids reliance on a single corporate sponsor, preserving the public‑good character.

A concrete case: the rollout of an open‑source telemedicine platform for rural primary health centres. The ethical analysis would map stakeholders (patients, ASHA workers, state health department, open‑source contributors), identify risks (data leakage through third‑party plugins, exclusion of non‑literate users, sustainability of community maintenance), and apply the four pillars. The decision would mandate a stewardship board with at least two patient‑representatives, a mandatory privacy‑by‑design audit before each release, a voice‑first interface in Hindi, Tamil, and Bengali, and a financing model where the National Health Authority contributes 60 % of operational costs while the remaining 40 % is sourced from a CSR‑linked innovation fund with a claw‑back clause if the platform is proprietary‑forked.

Examiners often test whether “open source” automatically equals “ethical”. The correct answer cites the 2021 “Kerala Open Data Portal” audit, which found that open datasets lacked metadata standards, leading to misinterpretation by local NGOs. The ethical response is not merely openness but governed openness — standards, stewardship, and accountability.

Applying the Principle of Non‑Discrimination in Public‑Sector AI Model Training Data Governance

Non‑discrimination under Articles 14, 15, and 16 extends to algorithmic systems when they influence public‑service access. The training data lifecycle — collection, labeling, augmentation, and versioning — is the primary site where historical bias becomes encoded. A rigorous governance protocol comprises: (1) Data Provenance Register — immutable ledger (e.g., blockchain‑anchored hash) recording source, consent status, and demographic composition of each dataset; (2) Disparate Impact Testing — statistical parity, equalized odds, and calibration metrics computed across protected attributes (caste, gender, disability, religion) before model training; (3) Bias Mitigation Pipeline — pre‑processing (re‑sampling, re‑weighting), in‑processing (adversarial debiasing), and post‑processing (threshold adjustment) steps documented in a model card; (4) Continuous Monitoring — automated drift detection on protected‑group performance metrics with a 30‑day alert threshold.

The 2023 “Delhi Transport Corporation Bus‑Allocation AI” pilot illustrates the stakes. The model, trained on historic ridership data, allocated fewer buses to routes serving predominantly Dalit neighbourhoods because past ticketing data under‑counted cash‑paying passengers. A disparate impact test revealed a 22 % lower service frequency for those routes. The remediation combined (a) augmenting training data with manual passenger counts, (b) adding a fairness constraint equalising service frequency across social groups, and (c) establishing a quarterly audit by the State Commission for Scheduled Castes.

In case‑study answers, candidates must reference the Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) judgment that read sexual orientation into Article 15, signalling that “protected characteristics” are expansive. They should also cite the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, which mandates accessibility in digital services. The decision template should include a Data Governance Charter signed by the data‑controller (e.g., Ministry of Social Justice), the Data Protection Officer, and an independent ethics auditor, with a sunset review after 18 months.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Use of Remote Sensing Data in Environmental Enforcement

Remote sensing — satellite imagery (e.g., ISRO’s Resourcesat‑2A, Sentinel‑2), aerial drones, and LiDAR — provides high‑resolution, time‑series evidence for forest cover loss, illegal mining, and water‑body encroachment. Ethical use demands a framework that respects procedural fairness, data accuracy, and community rights.
