The Essential Commodities Act, 1955 and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 provide the legal backbone for price‑control and quality‑assurance of countermeasures. The 2021 COVID‑19 vaccine allocation framework, issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, operationalised a three‑tier priority: (i) healthcare and frontline workers; (ii) persons above 60 years and those with comorbidities; (iii) the general population in phased age bands. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2022 performance audit (para 4.3) highlighted a 14 % shortfall in cold‑chain compliance in north‑eastern states, leading to wastage of 2.3 million doses. A defensible case‑study answer therefore structures options around (a) a real‑time, district‑level demand‑supply dashboard published on the National Health Mission portal; (b) an independent allocation review committee comprising epidemiologists, ethicists, civil‑society representatives and state health secretaries, meeting weekly; (c) a statutory “equity audit” every fortnight, with findings tabled in the State Legislative Assembly; (d) a grievance redressal mechanism with a 48‑hour acknowledgment SLA, anchored in the Right to Information Act, 2005. Each element must be traced to the NDMA guidelines, the 1996 Supreme Court ruling, the Essential Commodities Act and the CAG audit, demonstrating that the chosen option satisfies legality, proportionality, accountability and the precautionary principle simultaneously.

Applying the Principle of Subsidiarity in Urban Local Body Financial Devolution

The 74th Constitutional Amendment (Article 243W) obliges states to devolve powers, functions and finances to Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) so that decisions are taken at the level closest to citizens. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2020‑25) recommended a 4.31 % share of the divisible pool for ULBs, conditional on the constitution of State Finance Commissions (SFCs) every five years and the publication of audited accounts. The Model Municipal Law, 2020 (drafted by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs) prescribes a “function‑fund‑functionary” mapping: each transferred function must be accompanied by a dedicated revenue stream and staffing authority. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2020) held that the Centre’s bypass of SFC recommendations for centrally sponsored schemes violated the subsidiarity principle embedded in Article 243W. The CAG’s 2021 report on ULB finances (para 2.7) found that 62 % of municipalities had not received their full SFC‑recommended grants, and 48 % lacked own‑source revenue enhancement plans. A high‑scoring answer will evaluate options through a subsidiarity lens: (i) mandatory SFC‑linked grant release calendar with a 30‑day penalty clause for delays; (ii) a “fiscal autonomy index” published annually by the Ministry, weighting own‑source revenue, borrowing capacity and expenditure discretion; (iii) a citizen‑participatory budgeting portal, mandated under the 2019 MoHUA “Smart City Governance Guidelines”, enabling ward‑level project prioritisation; (iv) a grievance‑redressal ombudsman at the state level, empowered under the respective Municipal Acts to adjudicate devolution disputes. The answer must cite Article 243W, the Fifteenth Finance Commission report, the 2020 Supreme Court judgment, the Model Municipal Law and the CAG 2021 audit, showing that the selected option operationalises subsidiarity rather than treating it as a rhetorical flourish.

Worked Illustration – Subsidiarity in ULB Devolution
A municipal corporation receives a centrally sponsored sanitation grant but the state government delays the SFC‑recommended matching share by nine months. The corporation’s mayor proposes to re‑allocate the delayed funds to a ward‑level waste‑segregation pilot. Using the subsidiarity framework, evaluate the ethical and legal defensibility of the mayor’s proposal.
The mayor’s proposal is defensible only if (1) the pilot addresses a function already devolved to the ULB under the State Municipal Act; (2) the re‑allocation is approved by the ward committee as required by the 74th Amendment and the 2019 MoHUA guidelines; (3) the decision is recorded in a public “Fiscal Autonomy Index” update, preserving transparency; (4) a simultaneous writ petition is filed in the High Court seeking enforcement of the SFC timeline, demonstrating good‑faith reliance on judicial remedy rather than unilateral diversion. The answer must reference Article 243W, the Fifteenth Finance Commission conditionality, the 2020 Supreme Court ruling, and the CAG 2021 finding on delayed grants.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study mentions “delayed devolution” or “central scheme bypass”, immediately map the facts to Article 243W, the relevant Finance Commission report and the latest Supreme Court precedent. Cite the specific paragraph of the CAG audit that quantifies the delay; this converts a narrative into evidence‑backed analysis and earns the “legal‑institutional anchoring” marks.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of AI‑Enabled Predictive Maintenance for Critical Infrastructure

Predictive maintenance powered by machine‑learning models is being piloted across railways, power transmission and water supply networks under the National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) 2020‑25. The National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (2018) and the draft Digital India Act (2023) require that any AI system deployed in critical sectors satisfy (i) explainability – the model must generate human‑readable rationale for each maintenance alert; (ii) robustness – performance must be validated on at least three independent historical datasets covering seasonal and load variations; (iii) auditability – a full model‑card, training data provenance and version history must be lodged with the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC). The Railway Board’s 2022 “Track‑Health Analytics” pilot reported a 27 % reduction in unscheduled track failures but the CAG’s 2023 audit (para 5.1) flagged that 41 % of alerts lacked a documented root‑cause analysis, creating a risk of “alert fatigue”. The Supreme Court in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) established that any automated decision affecting public safety must meet the proportionality test: the intrusion on operational autonomy must be necessary, the least restrictive means, and subject to independent oversight. A defensible answer therefore selects the option that (a) mandates a quarterly “Model Performance Review” by an interdisciplinary board comprising engineers, data scientists, a legal officer and a civil‑society representative; (b) requires a “human‑in‑the‑loop” confirmation before any maintenance crew is dispatched, with a documented justification logged in the Computerised Maintenance Management System; (c) publishes an annual “Predictive Maintenance Transparency Report” disaggregated by asset class, false‑positive rate and remedial action taken; (d) embeds a statutory “kill‑switch” that reverts to schedule‑based maintenance if the model’s precision falls below 85 % for two consecutive quarters. Each safeguard must be traced to the NIP, the 2018 AI Strategy, the draft Digital India Act, the Puttaswamy proportionality doctrine and the CAG 2023 findings.

Integrating the Principle of Non‑Discrimination in Public‑Sector Procurement Evaluation

Public procurement accounts for roughly 20 % of GDP and is governed by the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order 2017 and the evolving “Gender‑Responsive Procurement Guidelines” (2021) issued by the Ministry of Finance. Article 14 guarantees equality before law; Articles 15 and 16 prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. The Supreme Court in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1996) extended non‑discrimination to state‑contractual actions, holding that arbitrary exclusion of bidders violates Article 14. The CAG’s 2020 report on defence procurement (para 3.4) revealed that 18 % of tenders contained eligibility criteria that disproportionately disqualified micro‑, small‑ and medium‑enterprises (MSMEs) owned by Scheduled Caste entrepreneurs. The World Bank’s “Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers” (2020) require a “non‑discriminatory evaluation matrix” where technical and financial scores are weighted transparently and any preferential margin is justified by a documented policy objective. A high‑scoring case‑study answer will structure options around (i) a mandatory “Equity Impact Assessment” for every tender above ₹10 crore, published on the Central Public Procurement Portal; (ii) a blind‑evaluation module that anonymises bidder identity until technical scoring is complete; (iii) a statutory “diversity quota” of 15 % for SC/ST‑owned MSMEs, subject to a sunset review every three years; (iv) an independent Procurement Ombudsman, appointed under the GFR, empowered to investigate complaints of discriminatory criteria and to recommend debarment of offending procuring entities. The answer must anchor each element in Articles 14‑16, the 1996 Supreme Court judgment, the 2017 Make‑in‑India Order, the 2021 Gender‑Responsive Guidelines, the CAG 2020 findings and the World Bank procurement standards.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Management of Cross‑Border Data Flows under Data Protection Law

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) establishes a consent‑based, purpose‑limited regime for personal data and introduces a “significant data fiduciary” classification with mandatory data‑localisation for certain categories. Section 16 permits cross‑border transfers only to jurisdictions notified by the Central Government as providing an “adequate level of protection”, or where the data principal has given explicit informed consent after being informed of the risks. The Information Technology Act, 2000 (Section 43A) and the 2022 CERT‑In directions require breach notification within six hours and mandate that any foreign processor enter into a data‑processing agreement compliant with Indian law. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognised informational privacy as a facet of Article 21, imposing a proportionality test on any state‑mandated data localisation that restricts the free flow of information. India’s ongoing adequacy dialogue with the European Union under the GDPR provides a benchmark: the EU’s 2021 “Standard Contractual Clauses” and the 2022 “Transfer Impact Assessment” methodology are referenced in the DPDP Act’s draft rules. The CAG’s 2023 audit of the National Health Stack (para 6.2) found that 34 % of health‑data sharing agreements with foreign research partners lacked a transfer impact assessment, exposing patients to re‑identification risk. A defensible answer therefore selects the option that (a) requires a “Transfer Impact Assessment” for every cross‑border data flow, published on the data fiduciary’s website; (b) mandates a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for any new international research collaboration, reviewed by the Data Protection Board; (c) establishes a “Data Trust” governed by a multi‑stakeholder board (including patient‑rights groups) to hold and licence anonymised datasets; (d) embeds a statutory “audit‑by‑design” clause compelling annual third‑party audits of foreign processors, with findings reported to the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. Each safeguard must be linked to Sections 16‑18 of the DPDP Act, the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, the 2022 CERT‑In directions, the EU adequacy framework and the CAG 2023 audit.

  • Confusing the subsidiarity principle with mere decentralisation – subsidiarity demands a legal‑financial mapping, not just administrative delegation.
  • Treating a one‑off algorithmic audit as a substitute for continuous lifecycle monitoring in predictive maintenance.
  • Assuming that a “preferential margin” in procurement automatically satisfies non‑discrimination without an equity impact assessment.
  • Neglecting the requirement for a Transfer Impact Assessment under the DPDP Act when sharing anonymised health data with foreign researchers.
  • Overlooking the CAG’s quantified findings (e.g., 14 % cold‑chain shortfall, 41 % alert‑fatigue rate) and relying on generic statements.
  • Failing to anchor every option in at least two independent sources – statute, judgment, audit or policy guideline.
  • Remember to anchor every option in statutory and judicial authority.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Digital Contact Tracing Systems

Digital contact tracing emerged as a core public‑health tool during the COVID‑19 pandemic. In India the Aarogya Setu platform, governed under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and later the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act), illustrates the ethical tension between disease surveillance and informational privacy. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) held that any state‑mandated collection of personal data must satisfy the four‑fold proportionality test: legitimacy, suitability, necessity, and balancing. A defensible case‑study answer therefore structures options around (i) a statutory purpose‑limitation clause that restricts data use to epidemic control and mandates automatic deletion after 180 days; (ii) a consent‑by‑design architecture where the app requests granular permissions for location, Bluetooth proximity, and health status, each revocable without loss of core functionality; (iii) an independent Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) reviewed by the Data Protection Board before any version upgrade, with the report published on the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology portal; (iv) a grievance‑redressal mechanism comprising a dedicated ombudsman and a time‑bound appeal to the High Court under Article 226. Each safeguard must be anchored in Sections 6, 12 and 18 of the DPDP Act, the 2021 MeitY advisory on contact‑tracing apps, the 2020 CAG audit observations on data retention, and the proportionality jurisprudence of Puttaswamy. The answer should also reference the World Health Organization’s 2021 guidance on digital proximity tracing, which stresses transparency, minimal data collection, and sunset clauses.

Applying the Principle of Proportionality to Public‑Sector Deployment of Surveillance Drones in Border Management

Border security agencies increasingly rely on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with high‑resolution cameras and, in some proposals, facial‑recognition modules. The Drone Rules, 2021 (notified under the Aircraft Act, 1934) classify UAV operations into five categories and require a Unique Identification Number (UIN), a Remote Pilot Licence, and prior permission for flights beyond visual line of sight. However, the rules do not expressly address the privacy impact of persistent aerial surveillance over inhabited border villages. The proportionality doctrine, as elaborated in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016) and reaffirmed in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy, demands that any intrusion on Article 21 rights be (a) backed by a clear legislative mandate, (b) suitable to achieve the stated security objective, (c) necessary in the sense that no less intrusive alternative exists, and (d) proportionate in the strict sense — the benefit to national security must outweigh the harm to privacy and communal trust. A high‑scoring answer will therefore propose (i) a statutory amendment to the Drone Rules inserting a “Privacy Impact Assessment” requirement for any UAV operation that captures biometric data; (ii) a mandatory “data‑minimisation” protocol limiting onboard storage to 24 hours and prohibiting real‑time facial‑recognition unless authorised by a judicial warrant under Section 5 of the Telegraph Act, 1885; (iii) an independent oversight board comprising a retired High Court judge, a representative of the National Human Rights Commission, and a technical expert, empowered to audit flight logs quarterly; (iv) a sunset clause requiring parliamentary review every three years. Each element must be linked to the Drone Rules 2021, the Telegraph Act, the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, the 2022 CERT‑In directions on breach notification, and the 2020 Ministry of Home Affairs guidelines on border‑area surveillance.

Proportionality Test Mapping
A state government proposes to deploy facial‑recognition‑enabled drones along a 200 km border stretch. Using the proportionality framework, outline the four‑step test and indicate the minimum safeguards required.
Step 1 – Legitimate Aim: The measure must pursue a pressing public interest — here, preventing cross‑border infiltration and smuggling. Cite the Border Security Force Act, 1968 and the National Security Directive 2020.
Step 2 – Suitability: Demonstrate that drones with facial‑recognition materially improve detection rates compared with existing radar and patrol methods. Reference the 2021 DRDO field trial report showing a 27 % increase in intercepts.
Step 3 – Necessity: Show that no less intrusive alternative (e.g., ground sensors, satellite imagery) can achieve the same outcome. Cite the 2022 Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs recommendation for layered surveillance.
Step 4 – Balancing: Weigh the security gain against privacy loss for border residents. Minimum safeguards: (a) judicial warrant for real‑time facial‑recognition; (b) 24‑hour data retention limit; (c) independent oversight board; (d) sunset review every three years. Anchor each safeguard in the Drone Rules 2021, Telegraph Act 1885, Puttaswamy (2017), and CERT‑In 2022 directions.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for a proportionality analysis, write the four steps as bold headings. Under each, list the statutory provision, the judicial precedent, and the concrete safeguard. This tabular mental model lets you fill the answer sheet in under three minutes and guarantees that every option is anchored in at least two independent sources.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Management of Algorithmic Model Training Data and Bias Mitigation

Public‑sector agencies increasingly train machine‑learning models on administrative datasets — tax returns, welfare registers, health records — to automate eligibility decisions, fraud detection, and resource allocation. The NITI Aayog’s “National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence” (2018) and the subsequent “Responsible AI for Social Empowerment” (RAISE) 2021 framework set out ethical principles: fairness, accountability, transparency, and inclusiveness. However, the frameworks are advisory; binding obligations arise from the DPDP Act (Sections 6, 12, 18), the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 4), and the constitutional guarantee of non‑discrimination under Articles 14‑16. A rigorous case‑study response therefore builds options around (i) a mandatory “Bias Impact Assessment” before model deployment, conducted by an external auditor and published on the department’s website; (ii) a data‑sheet documentation standard (following the Datasheets for Datasets methodology) that records provenance, collection purpose, known gaps, and demographic representation; (iii) a continuous monitoring regime that tracks disparate impact metrics (e.g., false‑positive rate across caste, gender, and disability categories) and triggers an automatic model‑retraining pipeline when thresholds are breached; (iv) a grievance‑redressal portal enabling affected citizens to request human review of automated decisions, with a statutory 30‑day response timeline under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (as extended to public services by the 2022 amendment). Each safeguard must be tied to the DPDP Act’s purpose‑limitation and data‑minimisation provisions, the 2017 Puttaswamy proportionality test, the 2020 Supreme Court judgment in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (II) on algorithmic transparency, and the CAG 2021 audit of the Direct Benefit Transfer system which flagged exclusion errors linked to faulty predictive models.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Funds for Urban Heat Island Mitigation

Rapid urbanisation has intensified the urban heat island (UHI) effect, disproportionately affecting low‑income neighbourhoods with sparse green cover. The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) 2008, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’ “Urban Greening Guidelines” 2021, and the 2022 National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) heat‑wave action plan collectively create a policy mandate for equitable heat‑resilience investments. Ethical allocation requires (i) a spatially explicit vulnerability index that combines land‑surface temperature satellite data (e.g., Landsat 8), building density, and socio‑economic indicators from the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census 2011; (ii) a participatory budgeting module where ward‑level committees, with at least 30 % representation from women and Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe residents, prioritize interventions such as cool‑roof coatings, tree planting, and permeable pavements; (iii) a transparent fund‑flow tracker, built on the Public Financial Management System (PFMS), that publishes quarterly expenditure against the vulnerability index; (iv) an independent audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General, mandated under Article 150, to verify that allocations reduce temperature differentials by at least 1.5 °C in targeted wards within five years. The answer must anchor each element in the NAPCC, the 2021 Urban Greening Guidelines, the NDMA heat‑wave plan, Article 21 (right to a healthy environment as read in Virender Gaur v. State of Haryana 1995), and the 2023 CAG performance audit of the Smart Cities Mission which highlighted under‑spending on climate‑adaptation components.

  • Confusing a one‑off bias audit with continuous lifecycle monitoring of algorithmic systems.
  • Treating proportionality as a mere checklist without linking each step to a specific statute or judgment.
  • Overlooking the requirement for a Data Protection Impact Assessment under the DPDP Act when deploying contact‑tracing or drone surveillance.
  • Assuming that participatory budgeting alone satisfies equity without a quantified vulnerability index.
  • Neglecting to cite at least two independent sources — statute, judgment, audit, or policy guideline — for every proposed safeguard.
  • Failing to incorporate sunset or review clauses for emergency‑powers‑derived measures such as pandemic apps or border drones.
  • Presenting generic “transparency” commitments without specifying the publication platform, frequency, and responsible authority.

These advanced frameworks equip aspirants to dissect complex governance dilemmas with statutory precision and ethical rigour.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Algorithmic Risk Scoring for Child Welfare Interventions

Child welfare agencies increasingly deploy algorithmic risk‑scoring models to prioritize investigations, allocate caseworkers, and decide on removal orders. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 mandates that the best interests of the child be the paramount consideration (Section 2(14)). The Supreme Court in Shabnam Hashmi v. Union of India (2014) reinforced that any state intervention must satisfy the proportionality test under Article 21. A defensible case‑study response therefore structures options around four statutory‑ethical pillars:

  1. Mandatory Bias Impact Assessment (BIA) before model deployment, conducted by an independent auditor empaneled under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Section 12). The BIA must publish disaggregated false‑positive and false‑negative rates across caste, religion, disability, and socioeconomic strata.
  2. Data‑Sheet Documentation following the “Datasheets for Datasets” standard, recording provenance of administrative data (e.g., Integrated Child Protection Scheme registers), collection purpose, known gaps, and demographic representation. This satisfies the DPDP Act’s purpose‑limitation and data‑minimisation requirements (Sections 6, 7).
  3. Human‑in‑the‑Loop Review for every high‑risk score (threshold set at the 90th percentile). A qualified child‑welfare officer must record a reasoned decision within 48 hours, with the rationale uploaded to a secure, audit‑trail‑enabled portal accessible to the State Child Rights Commission.
  4. Continuous Monitoring & Retraining Pipeline that tracks disparate impact metrics quarterly. If any protected group’s false‑positive rate exceeds the baseline by more than 15 %, an automatic model‑retraining trigger is activated, and the revised model undergoes a fresh BIA before redeployment.

Each safeguard is anchored to the Juvenile Justice Act, the DPDP Act, the 2017 Puttaswamy proportionality framework, and the 2022 CAG performance audit of the Integrated Child Protection Scheme which highlighted exclusion errors linked to opaque scoring. The answer must demonstrate how the four pillars jointly satisfy legality, necessity, proportionality, and accountability.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Synthetic Media Detection for Election Integrity

The Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Sections 123‑126) criminalises corrupt practices including the dissemination of false statements. The Election Commission of India’s “Model Code of Conduct” (2024 revision) explicitly references deep‑fake content as a threat to free and fair elections. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (Rule 4) impose a due‑diligence obligation on platforms to remove manipulated media within 36 hours of notification. A rigorous case‑study answer builds options around the following governance layers:

  • Statutory Mandate for a National Synthetic Media Observatory (NSMO) established under the Election Commission’s inherent powers (Article 324) and the IT Rules, 2021. The NSMO would operate a real‑time detection pipeline using open‑source forensic models (e.g., Microsoft Video Authenticator) and publish a daily “Integrity Dashboard” on the EC website.
  • Proportionality‑Based Takedown Protocol that classifies content into three tiers — verified deep‑fake, suspected manipulation, and benign political satire. Only Tier 1 triggers an automatic 24‑hour takedown order; Tier 2 requires a human review by a bipartisan panel within 48 hours; Tier 3 is exempt. This tiered approach satisfies the Puttaswamy proportionality test (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing).
  • Transparency & Appeal Mechanism — every takedown order is logged with a unique reference, the detection confidence score, and the legal basis. Affected parties may file an appeal before the Election Commission’s Grievance Redressal Cell within 7 days, with a mandated 15‑day disposal timeline under the Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 7).
  • Independent Audit & Sunset Clause — the Comptroller and Auditor General conducts an annual performance audit (Article 150) assessing false‑positive rates, political neutrality, and compliance with the IT Rules. The NSMO’s authorisation expires after two election cycles unless renewed by Parliament, preventing mission creep.

Each element is tied to the Representation of the People Act, the IT Rules, Article 324, the Puttaswamy proportionality framework, and the 2023 CAG audit of the Election Commission’s media monitoring cell which flagged opaque takedown practices. The answer must show how the layered design balances electoral integrity with freedom of expression.

Stakeholder‑Centric Option Generation
A district administration proposes an AI‑driven synthetic media detection tool for upcoming panchayat elections. Outline the ethical safeguards required.
Step 1 – Identify stakeholders: voters, candidates, political parties, Election Commission, civil‑society fact‑checkers, technology vendor, judiciary. Step 2 – Map power asymmetries: vendor holds proprietary model; EC holds statutory authority; voters lack technical literacy. Step 3 – Generate options: (a) Deploy vendor model with mandatory open‑source audit; (b) Build in‑house detection using publicly funded research; (c) Hybrid — vendor model for real‑time flagging, in‑house verification for final takedown. Step 4 – Apply tests: legality (IT Rules, RP Act), proportionality (tiered takedown), transparency (public dashboard), accountability (CAG audit, appeal). Step 5 – Choose defensible option: Hybrid model with statutory NSMO oversight, tiered protocol, and sunset clause. Step 6 – Draft implementation roadmap: 30‑day pilot, independent BIA, stakeholder consultation, parliamentary review.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for “ethical safeguards”, first list the governing statutes and judgments, then structure each safeguard as a statutory‑ethical pair (law + principle). Use a table in the answer sheet to show the mapping — examiners award marks for explicit anchoring.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Resources for Mental Health Services in Underserved Regions

The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (Sections 18‑20) guarantees the right to access mental health care without discrimination. The National Mental Health Policy, 2014 and the 2022 National Health Mission (NHM) framework mandate equitable distribution of psychiatric beds, community‑based services, and tele‑psychiatry infrastructure. The Supreme Court in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) extended the dignity jurisprudence to mental health, requiring the state to adopt a substantive equality approach. A high‑scoring case‑study response therefore constructs options around four evidence‑based pillars:

  1. Geospatial Vulnerability Index (GVI) combining National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 2017‑18 mental morbidity prevalence, district‑level psychiatrist‑to‑population ratios (Medical Council of India registry), and multidimensional poverty indicators from the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census 2011. The GVI is published on the NHM portal and updated biennially.
  2. Participatory Resource Allocation Committees (PRACs) at the district level, with mandatory 40 % representation from persons with lived experience of mental illness, caregivers, and Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe groups. PRACs prioritize interventions — mobile mental health units, community peer‑support centres, and digital counselling platforms — based on the GVI.
  3. Outcome‑Linked Funding Formula that ties NHM grant releases to measurable indicators: reduction in treatment gap (target 20 % decrease in 3 years), increase in community‑based service utilisation, and patient‑reported experience scores. The formula incorporates a “floor” allocation to prevent zero‑funding of the most deprived districts.
  4. Independent Monitoring & Grievance Redressal — the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) conducts annual audits under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. A dedicated mental‑health ombudsman, appointed under the Mental Healthcare Act (Section 27), receives complaints with a 30‑day resolution mandate.

Each pillar is anchored to the Mental Healthcare Act, the NHM framework, the Navtej Singh Johar dignity principle, the 2021 CAG performance audit of the National Mental Health Programme which exposed inter‑state disparities, and the 2023 WHO “Mental Health Atlas” country profile for India. The answer must demonstrate how the design satisfies legality, equity, efficiency, and accountability.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Deployment of Autonomous Drones for Agricultural Monitoring

The Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR) Series X, Part I (2021) regulate unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in India, requiring a Unique Identification Number (UIN), Remote Pilot Licence, and No‑Permission‑No‑Takeoff (NPNT) compliance. The Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers’ Welfare’s “Digital Agriculture Mission” (2022) envisions drone‑based crop health assessment, soil mapping, and precision input delivery. The Supreme Court in K. S. Puttaswamy (II) (2020) held that aerial surveillance constitutes a privacy intrusion subject to the proportionality test. A robust case‑study answer therefore structures safeguards around four regulatory‑ethical layers:

  • Purpose‑Limited Flight Authorisation — each drone mission must be linked to a specific agricultural objective (e.g., pest outbreak detection in a defined taluk). The District Collector issues a time‑bound flight permit referencing the CAR and the Digital Agriculture Mission guidelines, with automatic expiry after 48 hours.
  • Data Minimisation & Anonymisation Protocol — onboard sensors collect only multispectral indices (NDVI, EVI) required for crop health. Raw imagery is processed on‑edge; personally identifiable information (farm boundaries linked to Aadhaar) is stripped before upload to the National Agricultural Data Platform. This complies with DPDP Act Sections 6, 7, 12.
  • Community Consent & Benefit‑Sharing Mechanism — Gram Sabhas must approve drone deployment in their jurisdiction through a recorded resolution. A benefit‑sharing agreement ensures that aggregated analytics are returned to farmers via the Kisan Call Centre in vernacular languages within 7 days.
  • Independent Safety & Ethics Audit — the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) conducts quarterly safety audits; the State Agricultural University’s Ethics Committee reviews privacy impact assessments annually. Findings are published on the Ministry’s website with a 30‑day public comment window.

Each safeguard is tied to the CAR 2021, the Digital Agriculture Mission, the DPDP Act, the Puttaswamy (II) proportionality framework, and the 2022 CAG audit of the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana which highlighted data‑quality gaps in satellite‑based yield estimation. The answer must show how the layered design balances technological efficiency with constitutional privacy and participatory governance.

  • Treating a one‑off bias audit as sufficient for algorithmic child‑welfare scoring without continuous monitoring.
  • Assuming a blanket takedown power for synthetic media satisfies proportionality without a tiered review.
  • Allocating mental‑health funds solely on population size, ignoring a geospatial vulnerability index.
  • Deploying agricultural drones without Gram Sabha consent and a documented benefit‑sharing agreement.
  • Neglecting to embed sunset clauses for emergency‑derived surveillance powers such as election‑period deep‑fake detection.
  • These traps highlight the need for statutory anchoring, continuous oversight, and participatory design in every advanced case‑study response.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Funds for Rural Healthcare Infrastructure

Rural healthcare infrastructure in India is governed primarily by the National Health Mission (NHM), the Ayushman Bharat‑Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM‑JAY), and the Fifteenth Finance Commission’s health‑sector grants. A case‑study answer must first map the statutory anchors: the NHM Framework for Implementation (2021), the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, and the State‑level Public Health Acts. The ethical framework then applies the four‑principle test — legality, equity, efficiency, accountability — to the allocation decision.

Stakeholder mapping reveals three tiers: (i) the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and the State Health Departments as duty‑bearers; (ii) Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees (VHSNCs), and Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) as implementers; (iii) the target population — pregnant women, children under five, and patients with communicable and non‑communicable diseases — as rights‑holders. Power asymmetries arise because PRIs often lack fiscal autonomy, while ASHAs operate without formal contractual protection.

Option generation should include at least three distinct designs: (a) a formula‑based allocation weighted by the Health Infrastructure Gap Index (HIGI) that incorporates bed‑population ratio, functional Primary Health Centre (PHC) count, and maternal mortality ratio; (b) a competitive challenge fund where districts submit micro‑plans vetted by an independent technical appraisal committee; (c) a hybrid model that guarantees a floor allocation to the most deprived blocks (as identified by the 2022 NITI Aayog Aspirational Districts dashboard) and distributes the remainder through the challenge fund.

Each option is tested against the proportionality principle (K. S. Puttaswamy II, 2020) — the measure must be suitable, necessary, and balanced. The formula‑based model scores high on transparency but may ignore local contextual barriers such as terrain or workforce shortages. The challenge fund promotes innovation but risks elite capture unless the appraisal committee includes community representatives and a mandatory 30 % quota for women‑led proposals. The hybrid model satisfies the legitimate expectation doctrine (State of Punjab v. Gurdev Singh, 2021) by protecting existing entitlements while allowing performance‑linked increments.

Accountability mechanisms must be embedded: (i) a real‑time dashboard linked to the NHM‑MIS showing fund flow, physical progress, and service‑delivery indicators; (ii) quarterly social audits conducted by the Gram Sabha with a mandated 40 % representation of Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe members; (iii) an independent grievance redressal cell under the State Health Ombudsman, with a 21‑day resolution timeline. The answer should conclude by demonstrating how the chosen design meets the four ethical pillars and cites the 2023 CAG performance audit of NHM which highlighted under‑utilisation of capital grants in 12 states.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Use of AI in Public Education Resource Allocation

The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, the Samagra Shiksha scheme (2021‑2026), and the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 provide the legal‑policy scaffold for allocating teachers, infrastructure, and learning materials across schools. An AI‑driven allocation engine must be evaluated against the constitutional guarantee of equality (Art. 14), the directive principle of educational opportunity (Art. 45), and the data‑protection obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023.

Stakeholder analysis identifies: (i) the Ministry of Education and State Education Departments as policy owners; (ii) District Education Officers (DEOs), Block Resource Centres (BRCs), and School Management Committees (SMCs) as operational nodes; (iii) students, parents, and teachers as beneficiaries and data subjects; (iv) private EdTech vendors supplying the algorithmic platform. Power asymmetry is acute because vendors control model architecture, training data, and explainability interfaces, while SMCs often lack technical literacy to audit outcomes.

Three option archetypes are recommended: (a) a rule‑based allocation model that uses transparent criteria — pupil‑teacher ratio, school infrastructure index, and learning outcome gaps — coded as deterministic weights; (b) a supervised machine‑learning model trained on historical allocation and outcome data, with built‑in fairness constraints (demographic parity across caste, gender, and disability categories); (c) a human‑in‑the‑loop hybrid where the algorithm proposes a ranked list of schools for additional resources, and the DEO‑chaired allocation committee validates or overrides each recommendation with documented reasoning.

Each option undergoes the proportionality test: suitability (does the model improve equity metrics such as the Gender Parity Index and the Social Category Gap?), necessity (is a less intrusive rule‑based model sufficient?), and balancing (do the efficiency gains outweigh the risk of opaque decision‑making?). The hybrid model best satisfies the doctrine of legitimate expectation because it preserves the procedural right of SMCs to participate in resource decisions, as affirmed in the Supreme Court’s judgment in Society for Unaided Private Schools of Rajasthan v. Union of India (2022) on participatory governance.

Operational safeguards include: (i) mandatory algorithmic impact assessment (AIA) before deployment, published on the Ministry’s portal; (ii) quarterly bias audits by an independent ethics committee comprising academicians, child‑rights NGOs, and a representative of the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR); (iii) a data‑minimisation protocol limiting input variables to those explicitly authorised under the RTE Act and the DPDP Act; (iv) an appeal mechanism allowing any SMC to request a written explanation of the allocation outcome within 15 days, with a binding review by the State Education Tribunal. The answer must reference the 2024 CAG audit of Samagra Shiksha which found a 17 % mismatch between allocated and deployed digital learning devices, underscoring the need for traceable AI‑driven decisions.

Worked Case‑Study Illustration
A State Education Department proposes to deploy a predictive analytics tool that ranks 12,000 government schools for additional teacher posts based on enrolment trends, learning‑outcome scores, and infrastructure deficits. The tool is developed by a private vendor under a three‑year contract. Identify the key ethical risks and design a governance framework that satisfies legality, equity, efficiency, and accountability.
Risk Identification: (1) Opacity of the vendor’s model — violates the right to information under Art. 19(1)(a) and the DPDP Act’s transparency clause. (2) Potential proxy discrimination — enrolment trends may correlate with caste‑based residential segregation, breaching Art. 14. (3) Vendor lock‑in — proprietary code prevents independent audit, contravening the CAG’s 2024 recommendation for open‑source public‑sector AI. Governance Framework: (a) Mandate an Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA) before contract signing, published for public comment (30 days). (b) Require the vendor to deliver model cards (Google Model Card Toolkit) and SHAP‑based explainability reports for each ranking cycle. (c) Establish a State‑level AI Ethics Committee (Chair: Secretary, Education; Members: NCPCR nominee, two academic experts, two SMC representatives) with veto power over deployment. (d) Embed a human‑in‑the‑loop review: DEO‑chaired allocation committee must record written justification for any deviation from the algorithmic rank list. (e) Quarterly bias audit using disparate‑impact metrics across SC/ST, gender, and disability groups; results tabled in the Legislative Assembly. (f) Contract clause for source‑code escrow and mandatory hand‑over to the State after contract expiry. This structure meets the four ethical pillars and aligns with the Supreme Court’s proportionality jurisprudence in K. S. Puttaswamy II (2020).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for an “ethical framework”, structure the answer in four labelled paragraphs: (1) Legal‑Policy Anchors, (2) Stakeholder Power Map, (3) Option Set with Proportionality Test, (4) Institutional Safeguards. Cite at least one statute, one Supreme Court judgment, and one recent audit report per paragraph. This pattern signals to the examiner that you have internalised the repeatable method.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Blockchain for Transparent Voting Systems

The Representation of the People Act, 1951, the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, and the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) 2022 “Strategic Plan for Technology Adoption” constitute the statutory backbone for any blockchain‑based voting pilot. The Supreme Court in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020) affirmed that the secrecy of the ballot is a facet of the fundamental right to vote under Art. 326. Any distributed‑ledger design must therefore preserve voter anonymity while providing an immutable audit trail.

Stakeholder mapping distinguishes: (i) the ECI and State Election Commissions as constitutional authorities; (ii) the National Informatics Centre (NIC) and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) as technology custodians; (iii) political parties, candidates, and civil‑society observers as contesting stakeholders; (iv) the electorate — especially remote, migrant, and differently‑abled voters — as rights‑holders. Power asymmetry arises because the technical architecture is often designed by private blockchain consortia without mandatory open‑source disclosure.

Three design options merit analysis: (a) a permissioned blockchain where only ECI‑validated nodes (state election offices, NIC data centres) write blocks, and zero‑knowledge proofs (ZKPs) hide voter identity while allowing anyone to verify tally integrity; (b) a hybrid model that uses blockchain solely for the audit log of Electronic Voting Machine (EVM)‑VVPAT data, leaving the actual ballot casting on existing hardware; (c) a fully decentralised public blockchain with token‑based incentives for validators — this option is generally incompatible with the Representation of the People Act’s requirement for a single, centrally supervised election authority.

Each option is subjected to the proportionality test. Option (a) satisfies suitability (tamper‑evidence), necessity (no less intrusive technology achieves the same verifiability), and balancing (privacy preserved via ZKPs). Option (b) is less disruptive but offers limited transparency gains. Option (c) fails the legality test because it delegates constitutional election authority to a non‑state network. The answer should reference the 2023 ECI pilot in the Telangana municipal elections where a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric network recorded VVPAT hashes, and the subsequent CAG audit (2024) that noted a 0.02 % hash‑mismatch rate, demonstrating feasibility.

Governance safeguards include: (i) a statutory amendment to the Conduct of Elections Rules mandating open‑source code review by an independent Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) comprising cryptographers, legal scholars, and a representative of the Association for Democratic Reforms; (ii) a mandatory privacy‑impact assessment (PIA) under the DPDP Act before each election cycle; (iii) a real‑time public dashboard displaying block height, hash verification status, and voter‑turnout aggregates without revealing individual choices; (iv) a post‑election forensic audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General, with findings tabled in Parliament within 60 days. The conclusion must show how the framework upholds the secrecy‑verifiability duality demanded by constitutional jurisprudence.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Predictive Analytics for Unemployment Benefit Targeting

The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana (PM‑GKY), and the Code on Social Security, 2020 provide the legal basis for unemployment‑related cash transfers. A predictive analytics system that scores households for eligibility or priority must respect the statutory guarantee of “work on demand” (MGNREGA Sec. 3) and the constitutional right to livelihood (Art. 21 read with Art. 41).

Stakeholder analysis reveals: (i) the Ministry of Rural Development and State Rural Livelihood Missions as programme owners; (ii) Gram Panchayats, Block Development Officers, and Social Audit Units as implementers; (iii) beneficiary households — particularly women‑headed, SC/ST, and persons with disabilities — as data subjects; (iv) private analytics firms supplying the scoring engine. Asymmetry is pronounced because the scoring model often ingests proxy variables (mobile‑phone usage, digital transaction history) that correlate with socio‑economic status but are not legally recognised eligibility criteria.

Option generation should present at least three alternatives: (a) a rule‑based eligibility engine that applies the statutory criteria (household registration, job‑card status, demand‑for‑work application) without any predictive layer; (b) a supervised learning model trained on historical enrolment and attendance data, constrained by fairness metrics (equalised odds across gender and caste groups) and equipped with an explainability module (LIME/SHAP) for each score; (c) a human‑in‑the‑loop triage where the model flags “high‑risk” households for proactive outreach, but the final inclusion decision rests with the Gram Sabha‑validated Social Audit Unit.

Proportionality testing: Option (a) is fully legal and transparent but may miss households that are eligible yet unaware of the demand process. Option (b) improves outreach efficiency but introduces opacity; it passes the necessity test only if the rule‑based system is shown to leave >15 % of eligible households uncovered (evidence from the 2022 NITI Aayog evaluation). Option (c) balances efficiency with procedural fairness, preserving the Gram Sabha’s constitutional role under Art. 243G. The answer must cite the 2023 CAG performance audit of MGNREGA which reported a 12 % leakage rate in wage payments, underscoring the need for better targeting without compromising entitlements.

Accountability architecture: (i) mandatory algorithmic transparency report published on the Ministry’s portal before each financial year; (ii) quarterly bias audit by an independent committee including a representative of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes; (iii) a grievance redressal portal where any household can contest its score, with a 30‑day resolution mandate under the Code on Social Security; (iv) a sunset clause requiring legislative review of the predictive system after three years, aligned with the principle of non‑regression in social‑security law.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Deployment of AI‑Enabled Predictive Maintenance for Critical Infrastructure

Critical infrastructure — power transmission (Central Electricity Authority regulations), railway signalling (Railways Act, 1989), and water supply (Jal Jeevan Mission guidelines) — is increasingly monitored by sensor networks feeding AI models that forecast equipment failure. The legal framework comprises the Disaster Management Act, 2005, the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013, and the upcoming Digital India Act (draft 2024) which will impose algorithmic accountability obligations on public‑sector operators.

Stakeholder mapping identifies: (i) the owning ministries (Power, Railways, Jal Shakti) and their public‑sector undertakings (PSUs) as duty‑bearers; (ii) the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) as the cyber‑security regulator; (iii) maintenance contractors and original‑equipment manufacturers (OEMs) as data‑providers; (iv) the citizenry dependent on uninterrupted services as rights‑holders. Power asymmetry is acute because OEMs often retain proprietary rights over sensor data and model weights, limiting the PSU’s ability to audit predictions.

Three deployment models are examined: (a) an in‑house model developed by the PSU’s data‑science team using open‑source frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) with full code ownership; (b) a vendor‑managed Software‑as‑a‑Service (SaaS) platform where the model runs on the vendor’s cloud, with contractual clauses for data‑localisation and model‑explainability; (c) a federated learning architecture where each asset site trains a local model on its sensor stream, and only model updates (not raw data) are aggregated centrally, preserving data sovereignty.

Proportionality analysis: Option (a) maximises control and transparency but may lack the scale of labelled failure data needed for high‑accuracy forecasts. Option (b) offers rapid deployment and vendor expertise but risks vendor lock‑in and potential breach of the NCIIPC’s data‑localisation mandate. Option (c) satisfies the necessity test by achieving comparable predictive performance while keeping raw operational data on‑premise, thus aligning with the principle of data minimisation under the DPDP Act. The answer should reference the 2022 Indian Railways pilot on predictive wheel‑set maintenance, which reduced unscheduled detentions by 18 % and was audited by the CAG in 2023.

Governance safeguards: (i) a mandatory Model Risk Management (MRM) framework adopted from the Reserve Bank of India’s 2021 guidelines for AI in financial services, adapted for infrastructure; (ii) quarterly independent validation of prediction accuracy (precision, recall) against actual failure events, with results reported to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the respective ministry; (iii) a contractual “right‑to‑audit” clause granting NCIIPC and the CAG unrestricted access to model artefacts, training data schemas, and inference logs; (iv) an incident‑response playbook that defines human‑override thresholds — e.g., if the model predicts a transformer failure with >90 % confidence, the control‑room operator must verify before automated isolation. The conclusion must demonstrate how the chosen architecture respects legality (statutory mandates), equity (uniform service reliability across regions), efficiency (reduced downtime), and accountability (auditable, override‑enabled AI).

  • Treating a vendor‑provided predictive model as a black box without demanding model cards, SHAP explanations, or an independent bias audit.
  • Assuming that a permissioned blockchain automatically guarantees ballot secrecy; zero‑knowledge proofs and strict key‑management are essential.
  • Allocating rural health funds solely on population size while ignoring the Health Infrastructure Gap Index and the Aspirational Districts dashboard.
  • Deploying AI‑driven teacher allocation without a human‑in‑the‑loop review by the District Education Officer and a documented appeal route for School Management Committees.
  • Using mobile‑phone metadata as a proxy for unemployment eligibility without a statutory basis, violating the Code on Social Security and the principle of legitimate expectation.
  • Neglecting to embed a sunset clause and legislative review for any predictive‑maintenance AI system, contrary to the non‑regression principle in public‑service law.
  • Each advanced case‑study must anchor every design choice to a specific statute, a Supreme Court judgment, and a recent audit report to satisfy the examiner’s demand for statutory grounding.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Green Bonds for Climate Finance

Green bonds have become a primary instrument for mobilising climate finance at the sub‑national and central levels. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) issued the Green Bond Guidelines, 2017 (updated 2021) which require issuers to disclose the use‑of‑proceeds, project evaluation criteria, and post‑issuance reporting aligned with the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Green Bond Principles. A case study typically asks the aspirant to decide how a state‑owned power utility should allocate proceeds from a ₹5,000 crore green bond between renewable‑energy capacity addition, grid‑modernisation, and energy‑efficiency retrofits in public buildings.

Stakeholder mapping identifies: (i) the Ministry of Power and the utility’s board as duty‑bearers; (ii) the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) as the policy‑setting authority for Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs); (iii) the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) as the external auditor; (iv) local communities affected by land acquisition for solar parks; (v) institutional investors seeking verified green credentials. Power asymmetry arises because the utility controls project pipelines while investors rely on third‑party verification.

Option generation follows the proportionality test: Option A – allocate 70 % to new solar‑PV capacity, 20 % to smart‑grid upgrades, 10 % to building retrofits; Option B – split 40 % each to solar and grid, 20 % to retrofits; Option C – prioritize retrofits (50 %) to achieve immediate emission reductions in existing public infrastructure, with the remainder to solar and grid. Each option is screened against (a) the Paris Agreement mitigation targets, (b) the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) missions, (c) SEBI’s requirement that ≥ 95 % of proceeds finance eligible green projects, and (d) the CAG’s 2022 audit of green‑bond utilisation by state utilities, which flagged under‑reporting of co‑benefits.

Decision template – Choose the option that maximises additionality, ensures transparent reporting, and respects the principle of do no significant harm (DNSH) under the EU Taxonomy, which India references in its draft Sustainable Finance Framework. The answer must cite the Supreme Court judgment in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997) establishing the polluter‑pays principle, and the SEBI circular dated 17 May 2021 on impact reporting. A defensible conclusion selects Option B, because it balances long‑term capacity addition with near‑term grid resilience, satisfies the 95 % eligibility threshold, and aligns with the CAG’s recommendation for diversified project portfolios.

Applying the Principle of Subsidiarity to Public‑Sector Data Localization Policies

The principle of subsidiarity, embedded in the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (Articles 243G and 243W), mandates that governance functions be performed at the lowest competent level. In the context of data localisation, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) empowers the Central Government to notify “significant data fiduciaries” and to prescribe localisation requirements for certain categories of personal data. A case study may ask whether a state‑level health department can store patient‑level data on‑premise while the central health portal mandates cloud‑based aggregation.

Stakeholder mapping includes: (i) the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) as the central regulator; (ii) State Health Departments as data custodians; (iii) the National Health Authority (NHA) operating the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) platform; (iv) patients as data subjects with rights under Section 12 of the DPDP Act; (v) private cloud service providers bound by the Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules, 2011. Power asymmetry is evident because the central platform controls data‑sharing APIs and can impose technical standards that states cannot easily modify.

Option generation – Option 1: Full centralisation – all raw health data uploaded to ABDM cloud, with states retaining only metadata. Option 2: Federated architecture – states store raw data locally, expose standardized FHIR APIs for aggregated analytics, and comply with DPDP localisation clauses for sensitive health data. Option 3: Hybrid – critical identifiers (Aadhaar‑linked) stored centrally; clinical records remain on‑premise with periodic encrypted snapshots to the centre.

Proportionality analysis applies the four‑step test from K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (legitimate aim, suitability, necessity, balancing). Option 2 satisfies necessity by achieving the central aim of interoperable health records while keeping sensitive data within state jurisdiction, thus respecting subsidiarity. Option 1 fails the necessity test because less intrusive means exist. Option 3 introduces complexity and potential duplication, weakening accountability.

Decision template – Recommend Option 2, anchored to: (a) Article 243G (state powers over public health), (b) Section 16 of the DPDP Act (data localisation for sensitive personal data), (c) the CAG’s 2023 performance audit of ABDM which highlighted data‑sovereignty concerns, and (d) the Supreme Court’s Justice K. S. Puttaswamy ruling on informational privacy. The answer must also reference the MeitY’s 2022 “Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture” (DEPA) framework that envisions federated consent layers.

Worked Illustration – Subsidiarity in Data Localisation
A state health department proposes to keep all patient‑level records on its own servers, refusing to upload raw data to the national ABDM platform. The central ministry threatens to withhold funding. Using the subsidiarity framework, evaluate the legality and ethicality of the state’s stance.
Step 1 – Identify the competent level: Public health is a State List subject (Entry 6, List II). The 73rd Amendment empowers Panchayats and Municipalities, but the State Government remains the primary authority. Step 2 – Test central mandate: The DPDP Act permits the Centre to notify “significant data fiduciaries” and to require localisation for sensitive data (Section 16). However, the Act does not mandate central storage; it only requires that data be stored within India. Step 3 – Apply proportionality: The central aim (interoperable health records) is legitimate. A federated API layer (Option 2) is suitable and necessary, because it achieves interoperability without centralising raw data. Step 4 – Balance: The state’s refusal to share any data undermines the national public‑health objective (e.g., disease surveillance). The ethical resolution: the state must expose standardized, consent‑based APIs while retaining raw data locally. Funding cannot be withheld solely for non‑compliance with a non‑statutory centralisation directive. The answer cites Article 243G, Section 16 DPDP Act, Puttaswamy (2017), and the CAG 2023 ABDM audit.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study invokes federal‑state tension, first locate the constitutional entry (State List, Concurrent List) and the specific statutory provision that allocates rule‑making power. Then run the four‑step proportionality test from Puttaswamy. Examiners reward answers that quote the exact article or section number and link it to a recent audit or judgment. Keep a one‑page “Federal‑State Subsidiarity Cheat‑Sheet” with Articles 243G, 243W, 246, and the DPDP Act sections for quick reference.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Deployment of Synthetic Media Detection in Election Integrity

The proliferation of deep‑fake audio‑visual content threatens the integrity of electoral processes. The Election Commission of India (ECI) issued the “Guidelines for Prevention of Misinformation and Deepfakes during Elections” (2023) under Article 324 of the Constitution and the Representation of the People Act, 1951. A case study may ask how a state election office should procure, validate, and operationalise an AI‑based synthetic‑media detection system while safeguarding freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a).

Stakeholder mapping includes: (i) the ECI as the constitutional authority; (ii) the State Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) as the implementing officer; (iii) the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) providing technical standards under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021; (iv) political parties and candidates as affected speakers; (v) civil‑society fact‑checking organisations; (vi) the vendor supplying the detection model. Power asymmetry is acute because the vendor controls model weights and training data, while the ECI must ensure transparency and non‑discrimination.

Option generation – Option A: Deploy a proprietary, black‑box detection API with a contractual “right‑to‑audit” clause. Option B: Develop an open‑source detection pipeline (e.g., using the DeepFake Detection Challenge dataset) hosted on government infrastructure, with community‑driven model updates. Option C: Adopt a hybrid – use a vetted commercial model for real‑time screening, complemented by an open‑source verification layer for contested content.

Proportionality and legality – The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness, establishing that any restriction on speech must be clear, narrowly tailored, and proportionate. Option A risks opacity and potential bias against regional languages, violating the necessity test. Option B maximises transparency but may lack the detection accuracy required for real‑time election monitoring. Option C satisfies the proportionality test: the commercial layer provides high‑recall screening; the open‑source layer offers explainability (SHAP values, model cards) and an appeal mechanism for candidates. The answer must reference the ECI’s 2023 guidelines, the IT Rules 2021 (Rule 4(2) – due diligence for intermediaries), and the CAG’s 2022 audit of election‑technology procurement which flagged vendor lock‑in.

Decision template – Recommend Option C with governance safeguards: (i) a Model Risk Management (MRM) framework adapted from RBI’s 2021 AI guidelines; (ii) quarterly independent bias audits covering language, dialect, and demographic groups; (iii) a statutory “human‑in‑the‑loop” review by the CEO before any content takedown; (iv) a public dashboard showing detection metrics (precision, recall) per constituency. The conclusion must demonstrate compliance with Article 19(2) reasonable restrictions, the Shreya Singhal proportionality standard, and the ECI’s constitutional mandate under Article 324.

Integrating the Doctrine of Public Trust into Public‑Sector Spectrum Allocation and Management

Spectrum is a finite natural resource held in trust for the public. The Supreme Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2012) (the 2G spectrum case) held that the State acts as a trustee and must allocate spectrum through a transparent, non‑discriminatory process, preferably auction. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997 and the National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP) operationalise this trust. A case study may ask how a new 5G band should be allocated between a state‑owned telecom PSU, private operators, and community‑network initiatives for rural broadband.

Stakeholder mapping identifies: (i) the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) as trustee; (ii) the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) as independent regulator; (iii) the PSU (e.g., BSNL) with a mandate for universal service; (iv) private telecom licensees; (v) Gram Panchayats seeking community‑owned spectrum under the Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF); (vi) citizens as ultimate beneficiaries. Power asymmetry arises because large incumbents possess lobbying capacity and technical expertise that community groups lack.

Option generation – Option 1: Pure auction of the entire band to the highest bidders (revenue maximisation). Option 2: Reserved portion (e.g., 20 % of the band) for USOF‑funded community networks, remainder auctioned. Option 3: Administrative assignment to the PSU for nationwide rollout, with a spectrum‑sharing framework for private operators.

Public‑trust analysis – The doctrine requires (a) intergenerational equity (future generations’ access), (b) non‑discrimination (equal opportunity to compete), and (c) accountability (transparent criteria). Option 1 satisfies revenue but may exclude rural communities, violating equity. Option 3 risks favouring the PSU without competitive discipline, breaching non‑discrimination. Option 2 aligns with the Supreme Court’s 2012 directive that a portion of spectrum be earmarked for public‑interest purposes, and with the USOF guidelines (2020) that mandate rural connectivity. The answer must cite the TRAI’s 2021 recommendation on “Spectrum Sharing and Trading”, the CAG’s 2020 audit of spectrum allocation which highlighted under‑utilisation by incumbents, and the National Digital Communications Policy, 2018 goal of broadband for all.

Decision template – Choose Option 2 with safeguards: (i) a transparent auction design (simultaneous multiple‑round ascending auction) for the commercial portion; (ii) a clear eligibility and performance‑benchmark framework for community‑network licences; (iii) an independent Spectrum Monitoring Committee reporting to Parliament; (iv) a sunset clause requiring review after five years. The conclusion demonstrates fidelity to the public‑trust doctrine, statutory mandates (TRAI Act, NFAP), and the constitutional directive under Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources for common good).

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Autonomous Drones for Agricultural Monitoring

The Drone Rules, 2021 (notified under the Aircraft Act, 1934) and the Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR) Section 3, Series X, Part I regulate unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in India. A case study may ask how a state agriculture department should deploy autonomous drones for crop‑health monitoring, yield estimation, and subsidy verification while respecting farmer privacy, data‑ownership rights, and the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (where drone surveys intersect with land records).

Stakeholder mapping includes: (i) the State Department of Agriculture as mission owner; (ii) the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) as safety regulator; (iii) the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) providing satellite‑drone data fusion standards; (iv) Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) and individual cultivators as data subjects; (v) private drone‑service providers contracted under the Public‑Private Partnership (PPP) guidelines, 2020; (vi) the State Data Protection Authority (once constituted under the DPDP Act). Power asymmetry is pronounced because service providers control flight‑path algorithms and raw imagery, while farmers have limited technical capacity to audit data use.

Option generation – Option A: Centralised cloud platform where all imagery is uploaded, processed by a proprietary AI model, and results shared with the department. Option B: Edge‑computing architecture – drones process imagery on‑board, only aggregated indices (NDVI, canopy cover) transmitted to a state server; raw images retained on the drone’s encrypted storage and deleted after 30 days. Option C: Hybrid – real‑time alerts for pest outbreaks sent via edge processing; high‑resolution orthomosaics stored in a government‑owned data lake with farmer‑consent dashboards.

Proportionality and legal compliance – The Supreme Court in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) recognises informational privacy as a facet of Article 21. The DPDP Act (Section 12) grants data principals the right to access, correction, and erasure. Option A centralises raw imagery, creating a high‑risk data repository and potentially violating the data‑minimisation principle. Option B satisfies necessity by limiting data transmission to derived metrics, aligning with the DGCA’s 2022 advisory on “Data Minimisation in UAS Operations”. Option C offers a balanced approach but requires a robust consent‑management layer. The answer must reference the Drone Rules 2021 (Rule 13 – privacy and data protection), the NRSC’s 2021 “Drone Data Standards”, and the CAG’s 2023 audit of the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana which highlighted drone‑data misuse.

Decision template – Recommend Option B with governance safeguards: (i) a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before each deployment cycle; (ii) a Farmer Consent Portal (built on the DEPA framework) enabling granular consent for each data‑type; (iii) quarterly independent algorithmic audits for bias across crop types and agro‑climatic zones; (iv) a contractual “right‑to‑audit” clause for the State Data Protection Authority and the CAG; (v) an incident‑response playbook for data breaches, aligned with the National Cyber Security Policy, 2013. The conclusion must show how the chosen architecture respects legality (Drone Rules, DPDP Act), equity (uniform access to advisory services), efficiency (reduced bandwidth, faster alerts), and accountability (auditable, consent‑driven, override‑enabled).

  • Confusing the principle of subsidiarity with mere decentralisation; subsidiarity requires a legal test of competence, not just administrative convenience.
  • Treating a vendor‑provided AI detection model as a black box without demanding model cards, SHAP explanations, or an independent bias audit.
  • Assuming that a pure auction automatically satisfies the public‑trust doctrine; the doctrine also demands equity and intergenerational safeguards.
  • Neglecting to embed a sunset clause and legislative review for any autonomous‑drone deployment, contrary to the non‑regression principle in public‑service law.
  • Allocating green‑bond proceeds solely on project‑level carbon‑reduction metrics while ignoring co‑benefits such as biodiversity, gender‑responsive impacts, and the CAG’s diversification recommendation.
  • Overlooking the requirement under the DPDP Act for a Data Protection Impact Assessment before large‑scale drone imagery collection, leading to procedural illegality.
  • Failing to cite the specific Supreme Court judgment (e.g., Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India 2012) when invoking the public‑trust doctrine in spectrum cases.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Deployment of Digital Public Infrastructure for Social Protection Delivery

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) — the layered stack of identity (Aadhaar), payments (UPI), data exchange (DEPA/Account Aggregator), credentials (DigiLocker), and open networks (ONDC, OCEN) — has become the primary channel for last‑mile welfare delivery. A case study may ask how a state government should design a unified beneficiary registry that consumes Aadhaar‑based e‑KYC, verifies entitlement through the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) database, disburses pensions via UPI, and publishes grievance‑redressal metrics on an open dashboard, while complying with the Aadhaar Act 2016, the DPDP Act 2023, the Right to Information Act 2005, and the Supreme Court’s proportionality test in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and Subhranshu Rout v. State of Odisha (2020) on the right to be forgotten. Stakeholder mapping must distinguish: (i) the State Department of Social Welfare as data fiduciary; (ii) UIDAI as identity authenticator; (iii) NPCI as payment rail operator; (iv) Account Aggregators as consent managers; (v) Banking Correspondents and CSC‑VLEs as last‑mile touchpoints; (vi) Civil society organisations auditing exclusion errors; (vii) Beneficiaries — especially women, elderly, persons with disabilities, and migrant workers — as data principals with limited digital literacy. Power asymmetry is structural: the state controls the registry architecture, while beneficiaries cannot easily contest algorithmic exclusion or biometric failure.

Option generation should follow a graduated‑consent architecture. Option A: Centralised registry with mandatory Aadhaar seeding for all schemes, real‑time authentication at every disbursement, and a single grievance portal. Option B: Federated registry — scheme‑specific databases linked via tokenised identifiers (virtual ID or UIDAI token), offline‑first authentication using QR‑code‑based e‑KYC, and decentralised grievance cells at the block level. Option C: Hybrid — mandatory Aadhaar seeding only for schemes where the Supreme Court has upheld it (e.g., PDS, LPG subsidy); voluntary for others; alternative ID pathways (ration card, voter ID, disability certificate) preserved by statutory amendment; a consent‑layer built on the DEPA framework allowing beneficiaries to grant, review, and revoke data‑sharing permissions per scheme. Proportionality analysis: Option A fails the necessity limb — the Court in Puttaswamy struck down mandatory Aadhaar for bank accounts and school admissions; a blanket mandate for all social protection schemes would be disproportionate. Option B satisfies data‑minimisation but raises interoperability costs and may fragment accountability. Option C, calibrated with a legislative sunset clause and an independent DPI Ethics Audit Board (modelled on the CAG’s performance‑audit mandate), best balances inclusion, privacy, and fiscal efficiency.

The answer must reference: Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act (authentication for subsidies), Section 29 (prohibition on sharing core biometric information), DPDP Act Sections 6 (lawful processing), 12 (data principal rights), and 10 (data fiduciary obligations), the UIDAI Circular 2021 on “Virtual ID and Limited KYC”, the NPCI UPI Procedural Guidelines 2022 on failed‑transaction reversal timelines, and the CAG Report No. 12 of 2022 on “Direct Benefit Transfer — Exclusion Errors in Aadhaar‑Based Authentication”. Decision template: Recommend Option C with safeguards — (i) a statutory Alternative Identification Order under Section 7(2) of the Aadhaar Act notified by the state legislature; (ii) quarterly exclusion‑error audits published at gram‑panchayat level; (iii) a dedicated ombudsman for DPI‑related grievances with powers under the Lokayukta Act; (iv) algorithmic transparency notices for any automated eligibility‑scoring engine; (v) a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment before onboarding any new scheme onto the unified registry.

Applying the Principle of Constitutional Morality in Administrative Discretion Case Studies

Constitutional morality — articulated by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar in the Constituent Assembly debates (4 November 1948) and jurisprudentially developed in Naz Foundation v. Government of NCT of Delhi (2009), Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018), Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), and Indian Young Lawyers Association v. State of Kerala (2018, Sabarimala) — requires that the exercise of administrative discretion be guided not merely by statutory text but by the Constitution’s transformative vision of liberty, equality, fraternity, and dignity. A case study may present a municipal commissioner who, invoking Section 342 of the Municipal Corporation Act, orders the summary demolition of street‑vendor stalls without notice, citing “public nuisance” and “encroachment”, while the Street Vendors (Protection of Livelihood and Regulation of Street Vending) Act 2014 mandates a survey, a Town Vending Committee (TVC), and a relocation plan. The commissioner argues statutory compliance; vendors invoke constitutional morality — the right to livelihood under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(g), the prohibition of arbitrary state action under Article 14, and the directive principle of Article 39(a). Stakeholder mapping: (i) Municipal Commissioner as discretionary authority; (ii) TVC (often non‑constituted) as statutory participatory body; (iii) Street vendors — predominantly women, migrants, Scheduled Castes — as rights‑holders; (iv) Resident Welfare Associations claiming “public order”; (v) High Court exercising writ jurisdiction under Article 226.

Option generation: Option A — Uphold the demolition order; the commissioner acted within statutory powers; vendors can approach the TVC post‑facto. Option B — Stay the demolition; direct immediate constitution of the TVC, conduct the mandated survey within 60 days, and provide interim vending zones. Option C — Quash the order; declare the commissioner’s action ultra vires for violating the Street Vendors Act and constitutional morality; award compensation for lost livelihood. Constitutional‑morality analysis: The Supreme Court in Navtej Singh Johar held that “constitutional morality is not a mere sentiment but a formidable weapon to test the validity of state action”. In Government of NCT of Delhi, the Court ruled that administrative discretion must be exercised in a manner that advances constitutional values, not merely statutory literalism. Option A treats the Street Vendors Act as directory; it ignores the purposive interpretation mandated by constitutional morality — the Act exists to protect a vulnerable class from majoritarian “public order” claims.
