A district administration proposes to deploy an AI‑based beneficiary selection system for a nutrition scheme. Outline the algorithmic audit steps required under the DPDP Act and the MeitY Responsible AI guidelines, and explain how open‑source licensing of the model can enhance accountability.
Step 1 – Inventory & Classification: Register the model in the department’s Model Inventory Register (DPDP Act s.12). Classify as “high‑risk” because it determines access to food entitlements (fundamental right under Article 21).
Step 2 – Risk Tiering: Apply OECD AI Principles’ high‑risk criteria — impact on vulnerable groups (children, pregnant women), scale (district‑wide), irreversibility (exclusion leads to malnutrition).
Step 3 – Bias Testing: Run disparate‑impact analysis across caste, gender, disability, and geography using the Alkire‑Foster multidimensional poverty index. Document false‑negative rates for each subgroup; any rate exceeding 5 % triggers redesign.
Step 4 – Independent Audit: Engage a CAG‑empanelled auditor for a third‑party audit per IEEE 7001. Publish the audit summary on the district’s Algorithmic Transparency Register (quarterly update mandated by RTI Act).
Step 5 – Open‑Source Licensing: Release the model code under Apache 2.0 with an SPDX identifier. This enables (a) community scrutiny of feature engineering; (b) fork‑right for civil‑society to maintain a parallel “fairness‑enhanced” version; (c) compliance with GFR 158 open‑standard procurement. The OSPO established under MeitY’s 2021 policy oversees contribution governance and annual ethical impact review.
Outcome: The combined audit‑open‑source regime satisfies the proportionality test from Puttaswamy, the non‑arbitrariness standard under Article 14, and the DPDP Act’s purpose‑limitation principle, delivering a defensible, transparent decision.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study mentions an AI‑driven welfare tool, immediately map the four‑stage audit cycle (inventory → risk tier → bias test → independent audit) to the statutory anchors (DPDP Act s.12, MeitY guidelines, CAG Act). Pair each stage with a concrete artefact (model card, AIA, bias report, audit certificate). If the prompt asks for “enhancing accountability”, cite open‑source licensing (Apache 2.0) and the OSPO governance model — this scores both legal‑compliance and ethical‑design marks.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Management of Public Health Emergency Powers and Sunset Clauses

Emergency public‑health powers in India derive from the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 (EDA), the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (DMA), and the constitutional scheme of Article 21 (right to life) read with Article 19(1)(d) (freedom of movement). The Supreme Court in Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2020) held that any restriction on migrant workers’ movement must satisfy the “triple test” of legality, legitimate aim, and proportionality — the same framework that governs algorithmic restrictions under Puttaswamy. A robust ethical framework therefore requires: (1) Statutory Clarity — the executive order must cite the specific section (e.g., EDA s.2, DMA s.6) and define the geographical and temporal scope; (2) Sunset Clause — every emergency regulation must contain an automatic expiry date (maximum 30 days) with a mandatory parliamentary review before extension, mirroring the “sunset review” provision in the DMA s.35; (3) Least Restrictive Means — the state must demonstrate that non‑coercive alternatives (targeted testing, community‑based isolation) were considered and rejected with reasoned orders; (4) Data‑Protection Safeguards — health‑surveillance data collected under the EDA must comply with DPDP Act purpose‑limitation and storage‑limitation principles, and be deleted within 90 days of the emergency’s termination; (5) Accountability Mechanism — an independent “Public Health Emergency Oversight Committee” (PHEOC) comprising a retired High Court judge, a public‑health expert, a civil‑society representative, and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s nominee, meets fortnightly to audit orders and publish a compliance dashboard.

The WHO’s “Public Health Emergency (PHE) Framework” (2022) and India’s National Health Mission (NHM) guidelines reinforce the principle of “non‑regression” — emergency measures must not permanently erode baseline health‑system capacities. In practice, the 2020 COVID‑19 ordinances (e.g., the Epidemic Diseases (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020) lacked explicit sunset dates, prompting judicial intervention. The aspirant’s decision template should therefore embed: (a) a “Sunset Review Calendar” with fixed parliamentary debate dates; (b) a “Proportionality Impact Statement” quantifying the restriction’s effect on livelihoods (using Periodic Labour Force Survey data); (c) a “Data Deletion Protocol” certified by the Data Protection Officer; (d) a “Grievance Redressal Tracker” linked to the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS). This structure converts abstract constitutional doctrine into auditable administrative action.

Applying the Principle of Substantive Due Process in Administrative Discretion Cases

Indian administrative law has migrated from a thin “procedure established by law” (Article 21) to a substantive due‑process standard through a trilogy of judgments: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) — fairness, reasonableness, and non‑arbitrariness are implicit in Article 21; K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — privacy as a fundamental right demands a “just, fair and reasonable” procedure; Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) — “manifest arbitrariness” under Article 14 invalidates executive action that lacks a rational nexus. The Wednesbury unreasonableness test (UK) remains persuasive but Indian courts now apply a stricter “proportionality” analysis: (i) legitimate aim; (ii) suitable means; (iii) necessary in a democratic society; (iv) balancing of rights. The doctrine of legitimate expectation (from Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corp., 1993) further requires that a promise or consistent practice creates a procedural right to be heard before withdrawal.

A case‑study checklist for the aspirant: (1) Identify the statutory source of discretion (e.g., Section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act, 2013). (2) Verify whether the statute prescribes criteria or leaves it “unfettered”. (3) Apply the “manifest arbitrariness” test — does the order reveal a reasoning vacuum? (4) Conduct a proportionality matrix — list the aim, the measure, the less‑restrictive alternative, and the rights impacted (Article 19(1)(g) livelihood, Article 21 dignity). (5) Check for a reasoned speaking order — the Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2022) mandated that every discretionary order must record reasons. (6) Assess legitimate expectation — has the department issued a circular or established a consistent practice that the applicant relied upon? (7) Prescribe remedy — quash, remand with directions, or issue a mandamus for a fresh decision within a fixed timeline. This structured approach converts the abstract “substantive due process” into a repeatable analytical scaffold that examiners reward.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Spectrum and Frequency Resources

Spectrum is a finite natural resource governed by the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, and the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997 (TRAI Act). The National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP), revised periodically by the Wireless Planning and Coordination Wing (WPC), allocates bands for defence, broadcasting, mobile, satellite, and scientific use. Allocation methodology shifted from “first‑come‑first‑served” (FCFS) to Simultaneous Multiple Round Auctions (SMRAs) after the Supreme Court’s 2012 judgment in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2G Spectrum Case), which held that natural resources must be distributed through transparent, market‑based mechanisms to satisfy Article 14 and the Directive Principle of State Policy under Article 39(b). The ethical framework for spectrum allocation therefore rests on three pillars: (1) Efficient Use — technical parameters (spectral efficiency, carrier aggregation) must be benchmarked against ITU‑R recommendations; (2) Equitable Access — the Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF) finances rural broadband; spectrum caps (e.g., 25 % of total assigned spectrum per licensee in a band) prevent monopolisation; (3) Public Interest — revenue maximisation cannot trump digital inclusion; the 2022 5G auction reserved 600 MHz for “public‑interest” deployments (e.g., tele‑medicine, agritech) at a discounted reserve price.

Emerging issues include spectrum sharing and trading (Guidelines 2015), satellite spectrum for low‑earth‑orbit constellations (OneWeb, Starlink), and the “spectrum‑for‑satellite” debate where the Department of Space and TRAI coordinate under the Spacecom Policy 2020. The CAG’s 2021 “Spectrum Audit” highlighted under‑utilisation in the 2.3 GHz band, prompting a re‑farming exercise. An aspirant’s decision template should capture: (a) a “Spectrum Efficiency Scorecard” for each applicant (throughput per MHz, coverage obligation fulfilment); (b) a “Digital Inclusion Index” weighting rural coverage, affordability, and local‑language content; (c) a “Sunset Review Clause” in every licence — mandatory reassessment after 10 years with option to reclaim under‑used blocks; (d) a “Conflict‑of‑Interest Register” for the Spectrum Management Committee (SMC) members, aligned with the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2020. This ensures that the allocation process survives judicial scrutiny under the “manifest arbitrariness” and “proportionality” standards.

  • Treating algorithmic audit as a one‑time compliance checkbox rather than a continuous 18‑month cycle mandated by the CAG and IEEE 7001.
  • Assuming open‑source licensing alone guarantees accountability without an OSPO, community governance charter, and biennial ethical impact review.
  • Drafting emergency health orders without an explicit sunset date, parliamentary review trigger, and data‑deletion protocol, inviting Article 21 challenges.
  • Applying only the Wednesbury test while ignoring the Supreme Court’s proportionality matrix and manifest‑arbitrariness standard under Article 14.
  • Evaluating spectrum bids solely on revenue, neglecting the USOF‑linked digital inclusion index and the mandatory 10‑year sunset review.
  • Omitting the conflict‑of‑interest register for the Spectrum Management Committee, a gap the CAG’s 2021 audit explicitly flagged.
  • Failing to embed a reasoned speaking order in every discretionary decision, contrary to the 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam mandate.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Inter‑State Water Resources

Inter‑state water disputes are governed primarily by the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act, 1956, which empowers the Centre to constitute tribunals whose awards become binding after publication in the Official Gazette. The constitutional backdrop is Article 262, which bars the Supreme Court from adjudicating such disputes, and the River Boards Act, 1956, which provides for basin‑level coordination. Ethical analysis must therefore begin with a statutory mapping: identify the tribunal award, the gazette notification date, and any subsequent Supreme Court clarification (e.g., the 2018 Cauvery judgment that upheld the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal’s final award while directing a “water‑sharing formula” for distress years).

Stakeholder mapping in this context extends beyond the riparian states to include downstream communities, agricultural collectives, industrial users, and ecological entities such as wetlands protected under the Ramsar Convention. Power asymmetries often arise when a upstream state controls dam releases; the ethical framework must therefore test each allocation option against the principles of equitable utilisation (Helsinki Rules, 1966) and the “no‑significant‑harm” rule, both of which have been cited by Indian tribunals as persuasive international norms.

Option generation should follow a structured matrix: (1) strict adherence to the tribunal award; (2) a distress‑year adjustment formula agreed by a joint technical committee; (3) a market‑based water‑trading pilot with caps to protect smallholders; (4) a basin‑wide integrated water‑resources management (IWRM) plan with a permanent river‑board secretariat. Each option is evaluated through a proportionality test — legitimate aim (food security, drinking water, ecosystem health), suitability, necessity (least restrictive means), and balancing of rights (Article 21 right to water, Article 14 equality). The decision template must record a speaking order that references the specific tribunal clause, the hydrological data set (e.g., Central Water Commission’s 10‑year average flows), and the reasoning for any deviation.

Judicial anchors include the Supreme Court’s 2020 order in State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu directing the Cauvery Water Management Authority to publish real‑time release data, and the 2022 judgment in Maharashtra v. Gujarat (Narmada) reinforcing the duty to consult affected gram panchayats before altering release schedules. These precedents convert abstract equity into enforceable procedural duties that examiners expect to see cited.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Emergency Health Powers and Sunset Clauses

The legal basis for emergency health interventions rests on the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, the Disaster Management Act, 2005, and the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines. During COVID‑19, the Centre invoked Section 2 of the 1897 Act and Section 6 of the 2005 Act to issue lockdown orders, vaccination mandates, and data‑collection directives. Ethical scrutiny requires a three‑step protocol: (1) verify that the enabling statute expressly authorises the measure; (2) confirm that the order contains a sunset clause or a parliamentary review trigger; (3) assess proportionality against fundamental rights — Article 19(1)(d) movement, Article 21 life and personal liberty, and Article 14 non‑discrimination.

The Supreme Court in Alakh Alok Srivastava v. Union of India (2021) held that any restriction on movement must be “reasonable, necessary and proportionate” and must be reviewed at intervals not exceeding 30 days. The Court further mandated that data‑collection apps (e.g., Aarogya Setu) incorporate a data‑deletion protocol upon mission completion. A decision template for emergency orders therefore includes: (a) a “Sunset Review Calendar” with fixed dates for parliamentary committee scrutiny; (b) a “Least Restrictive Alternative” column comparing lockdown, night curfew, and targeted containment zones; (c) a “Rights Impact Matrix” scoring each measure on a 0‑5 scale for Articles 19, 21, 14; (d) a “Data Governance Annex” specifying storage location, access controls, and deletion timeline.

Stakeholder mapping must capture vulnerable groups — migrant workers, persons with disabilities, and informal‑sector women — whose voice is often absent in top‑down orders. The ethical escalation protocol requires a designated “Emergency Ethics Officer” in each state health department, empowered to pause implementation if the proportionality matrix flags a score above a pre‑set threshold. This institutional safeguard mirrors the NDMA’s 2020 directive for “Ethical Review Committees” at district level.

Worked Case: Designing a Sunset‑Enabled Lockdown Order
A state government proposes a 21‑day lockdown under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, without a statutory sunset clause. The order also mandates compulsory installation of a contact‑tracing app with no data‑deletion provision. Using the framework above, produce a concise speaking order that satisfies the Supreme Court’s proportionality and sunset requirements.
Speaking Order (excerpt): “Whereas the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897, Section 2 empowers the State to take special measures, the order shall remain in force for 21 days from 01‑May‑2025 and shall automatically lapse unless extended by a resolution of the State Legislative Assembly passed within 15 days of expiry (Sunset Review Calendar). The lockdown is limited to containment zones identified by the District Health Committee based on a 7‑day positivity rate >10 % (Least Restrictive Alternative). Movement for essential services, medical emergencies, and agricultural activities is expressly permitted (Article 19(1)(d) balancing). The contact‑tracing app shall store data on NIC‑certified servers, access restricted to the State Health Secretary, and all personal data shall be purged within 30 days of the order’s lapse (Data Governance Annex). A proportionality matrix (Annex‑A) scores the measure 2/5 on Article 19, 1/5 on Article 21, and 0/5 on Article 14, confirming necessity. The Emergency Ethics Officer shall review the matrix on Day 7 and Day 14 and may recommend modification.”
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for an emergency order, always draft a mini‑speaking order in the answer: cite the enabling section, embed a sunset date, list the least restrictive alternative, and attach a proportionality matrix. Examiners award marks for the “structured speaking order” format even if the narrative is brief.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Open Data Platforms and Civic Innovation

The National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP), 2012, and the Open Government Data (OGD) Platform (data.gov.in) constitute the statutory‑policy backbone for public‑sector data release. The Right to Information Act, 2005, provides the demand‑side right, while the NDSAP supplies the supply‑side mandate for proactive disclosure in machine‑readable formats. Ethical governance of these platforms requires a layered framework: (1) Legal Compliance — verify that each dataset carries a valid licence (e.g., Open Government Licence‑India, compatible with Creative Commons BY 4.0); (2) Privacy Safeguards — apply the “de‑identification” standard prescribed by the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023 (Section 3(2) on anonymisation) before publishing granular health or education data; (3) Equity Audit — assess whether the data catalogue reflects the needs of marginalized communities (e.g., caste‑disaggregated sanitation data) and whether APIs are accessible in regional languages.

Stakeholder mapping includes data custodians (line ministries), intermediary civic‑tech organisations, academic researchers, and end‑users such as gram panchayats planning water budgets. Power asymmetry arises when high‑value datasets (land records, procurement contracts) are released only in PDF, limiting machine reuse. The ethical decision template therefore mandates a “Format‑Readiness Scorecard” (CSV/JSON/API availability, metadata completeness, update frequency) and a “Civic‑Innovation Impact Metric” (number of verified applications built, documented service‑delivery improvements).

Judicial anchors: the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) recognised informational privacy as a facet of Article 21, requiring purpose‑limitation even for open data. The Delhi High Court in Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2020) directed the Ministry of Rural Development to publish MGNREGA wage data in open format within six months. These rulings convert the policy aspiration of “open by default” into a justiciable duty.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Procurement of Green Technology

Green public procurement (GPP) in India is guided by the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017, the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017 amendments on “life‑cycle costing”, and the Ministry of Finance’s 2021 “Green Procurement Guidelines” which mandate a minimum 20 % weight for environmental criteria in technical evaluation. The ethical framework integrates three pillars: (1) Environmental Integrity — apply the Life‑Cycle Assessment (LCA) methodology (ISO 14040/44) to compare bids on carbon footprint, water use, and end‑of‑life recyclability; (2) Social Equity — enforce the “Local Content” clause to ensure MSMEs and women‑led enterprises receive a fair share, aligned with the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006; (3) Fiscal Responsibility — use the “Total Cost of Ownership” (TCO) model rather than lowest‑bid price, preventing hidden future costs (e.g., battery replacement for electric buses).

Option generation for a municipal electric‑bus tender might include: (A) outright purchase with 10‑year warranty; (B) operating lease with performance‑based payments; (C) public‑private partnership where the private operator finances, operates, and maintains the fleet under a concession agreement. Each option is scored on a “Green Procurement Matrix” covering carbon intensity (kg CO₂e/km), local employment (jobs created per ₹ crore), and contract flexibility (termination clauses). The decision must be recorded in a speaking order referencing the specific GFR rule (Rule 173‑iii on life‑cycle costing) and the 2021 Guidelines’ “Environmental Weightage” clause.

Accountability mechanisms: the Central Vigilance Commission’s 2022 circular requires a “Green Procurement Audit” within 12 months of contract award, and the Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2023 report on “Sustainable Procurement” flagged the absence of post‑award verification of claimed emission reductions. Embedding a mandatory third‑party verification clause in the contract closes this gap.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Satellite‑Based Environmental Monitoring

India’s remote‑sensing capacity rests on the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), which operate the Bhuvan geoportal and supply data to the Forest Survey of India (FSI) for the biennial “India State of Forest Report”. The legal framework includes the Space Activities Bill (draft, 2017), the National Remote Sensing Policy, 2011, and the Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, which mandates satellite‑based monitoring for Category A projects. Ethical governance demands: (1) Data Integrity — adopt the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) “Quality Assurance Framework” for radiometric calibration; (2) Transparency — publish acquisition schedules, processing levels (Level‑1, Level‑2), and validation reports on the Bhuvan portal; (3) Equitable Access — provide free, open‑licensed (CC‑BY 4.0) access to panchayat‑level forest‑cover change maps, enabling community‑based monitoring under the Forest Rights Act, 2006.

Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), state forest departments, tribal gram sabhas, and private agri‑tech firms seeking precision‑farming inputs. Power asymmetry appears when high‑resolution (≤1 m) data is licensed commercially while coarse (30 m) data remains free, limiting local enforcement. The ethical decision template therefore requires a “Resolution‑Access Matrix” that specifies which resolution tiers are open, which are restricted, and the justification (national security, commercial confidentiality) for each restriction.

Judicial anchors: the National Green Tribunal in Vardhaman Kaushik v. Union of India (2021) ordered the MoEFCC to integrate satellite‑derived fire‑alert data into the real‑time forest‑fire management system. The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (2022) directed the NRSC to share raw SAR (Synthetic Aperture Radar) data for illegal mining detection in the Aravalli range. These orders translate technical capability into enforceable environmental stewardship duties.

  • Assuming that a tribunal award alone resolves inter‑state water equity without a distress‑year formula or real‑time release transparency.
  • Issuing emergency health orders without an explicit sunset date, parliamentary review trigger, and data‑deletion protocol.
  • Publishing open datasets only in PDF or proprietary formats, thereby defeating the machine‑readability mandate of NDSAP.
  • Evaluating green procurement bids solely on upfront price while ignoring life‑cycle costing and local‑content weightage prescribed by GFR and the 2021 Guidelines.
  • Restricting high‑resolution satellite data to commercial licences without a documented national‑security justification, contravening the Forest Rights Act’s community‑monitoring provision.
  • Failing to embed a proportionality matrix and speaking order in every discretionary decision, contrary to the Supreme Court’s 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam mandate.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Distributed Ledger Technology for Procurement Transparency

Distributed ledger technology (DLT) offers an immutable audit trail for every stage of public procurement — from tender publication to contract execution and payment release. The General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, Rule 173‑iii, mandates life‑cycle costing, while the 2021 Guidelines on Sustainable Public Procurement require an “Environmental Weightage” clause. Embedding DLT into the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) satisfies both by recording bid hashes, evaluation scores, and amendment logs on a permissioned blockchain anchored to the National Informatics Centre (NIC) root of trust. Stakeholder mapping identifies the procuring entity, the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), vendors (especially MSMEs), and civil‑society watchdogs. Power asymmetry arises when large vendors can influence offline negotiations; DLT mitigates this by forcing all communications onto a tamper‑evident ledger accessible to the CVC’s “Green Procurement Audit” mandated by its 2022 circular. Option generation includes (A) a full‑stack blockchain on Hyperledger Fabric with smart‑contract‑driven automatic bid‑opening; (B) a hybrid model where only critical events (bid submission, evaluation, award) are hashed to a public‑verifiable Merkle root; (C) a pilot limited to high‑value infrastructure contracts (>₹500 crore). Each option is scored on a “Transparency‑Cost Matrix” covering ledger latency (seconds), on‑chain storage cost (₹/GB), and vendor onboarding effort (person‑days). The decision must be recorded in a speaking order citing GFR 173‑iii, the 2021 Guidelines’ Environmental Weightage, and the Supreme Court’s 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam proportionality mandate. Accountability mechanisms: the CVC’s 2022 circular requires a post‑award DLT audit within twelve months; the CAG’s 2023 “Sustainable Procurement” report flagged missing verification of on‑chain emission‑reduction claims, which is closed by a mandatory third‑party oracle attestation clause in the smart contract.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Pandemic‑Response Medical Resources

The COVID‑19 pandemic exposed gaps in the ethical allocation of scarce medical resources — oxygen, ventilators, antiviral drugs, and vaccine doses. The legal backbone comprises the Disaster Management Act 2005 (Section 38), the Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 (Section 2), and the National Health Mission’s “Essential Health Services” framework. The Supreme Court’s 2021 suo‑motu order in In Re: Distribution of Essential Supplies directed states to adopt a “fair, transparent, and needs‑based” allocation protocol. An ethical framework for such allocation rests on three pillars: (1) Utilitarian maximisation — save the maximum number of life‑years using a validated Clinical Frailty Scale; (2) Prioritarian equity — give weighted priority to vulnerable groups (elderly, comorbidities, socially disadvantaged) consistent with the National Policy for Older Persons 2011 and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016; (3) Procedural fairness — publish real‑time allocation dashboards, enable grievance redressal through the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), and embed a sunset clause that triggers parliamentary review after 90 days. Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), state health departments, private hospitals, pharmaceutical manufacturers, and community‑based organisations. Power asymmetry appears when private hospitals hoard stock; the ethical decision template therefore requires a “Resource‑Allocation Matrix” that specifies (a) eligibility criteria, (b) allocation algorithm (e.g., weighted lottery), (c) audit checkpoints (daily stock reconciliation, weekly independent audit). Options for oxygen distribution might be: (A) centralised allocation by MoHFW based on district case‑load projections; (B) decentralised allocation by DDMA with real‑time data feed from the CoWIN platform; (C) a hybrid model where the centre sets quotas and districts manage last‑mile logistics. Each option is evaluated on the “Equity‑Efficiency‑Accountability” triad using a scoring rubric (0‑5). The final speaking order must reference the Disaster Management Act 2005, the Supreme Court’s 2021 order, and the 2022 CVC circular on “Emergency Procurement Transparency”.

Technique: Structured Ethical Option Scoring
A state government must allocate 10,000 vials of a scarce antiviral drug during a surge. Three options are on the table: (1) allocate proportionally to reported active cases; (2) allocate using a vulnerability index that weights age, comorbidity, and socioeconomic deprivation; (3) allocate by a lottery among all eligible hospitals. Using the Equity‑Efficiency‑Accountability triad, score each option (0‑5) and recommend the defensible choice with a speaking‑order rationale.
Scoring:
Option 1 – Equity 2, Efficiency 4, Accountability 3 → Total 9.
Option 2 – Equity 5, Efficiency 3, Accountability 4 → Total 12.
Option 3 – Equity 3, Efficiency 2, Accountability 5 → Total 10.
Recommendation: Option 2. It maximises prioritarian equity (protecting the most vulnerable), retains reasonable efficiency by targeting clinical need, and scores high on accountability because the vulnerability index is published, auditable, and subject to DDMA grievance review. The speaking order cites Disaster Management Act 2005 §38, Supreme Court In Re: Distribution of Essential Supplies (2021), and CVC 2022 Emergency Procurement Circular, and records the scoring matrix as an annex.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for “ethical allocation”, always structure the answer in three moves: (1) name the governing statutes and judicial orders; (2) lay out the ethical pillars (utilitarian, prioritarian, procedural) in a table; (3) present a scored option matrix and a speaking‑order paragraph that quotes the exact legal provisions. This pattern signals to the examiner that you can move from principle to enforceable decision.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Use of Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Sentencing Support

AI‑assisted sentencing tools — risk‑assessment algorithms, precedent‑retrieval engines, and predictive analytics — are being piloted in the e‑Courts Phase III project under the Supreme Court’s 2023 “Guidelines on Responsible AI in the Judiciary”. The constitutional anchor is Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty) read with the K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) privacy jurisprudence, which demands that any automated decision affecting liberty be transparent, explainable, and subject to human review. The statutory framework includes the Information Technology Act 2000 (Section 43A on reasonable security practices) and the forthcoming Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (Section 12 on algorithmic transparency). An ethical framework for deployment comprises four tests: (1) Explainability — the model must output a natural‑language rationale for each risk score, auditable by the National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG); (2) Bias Audit — an independent third‑party (e.g., Indian Statistical Institute) must evaluate disparate impact across caste, gender, and religion before go‑live and quarterly thereafter; (3) Human‑in‑the‑Loop — the presiding judge retains final discretion, documented in a “Sentencing Reasoning Sheet” that references the AI output and the judge’s independent reasoning; (4) Proportionality & Sunset — the tool’s use is limited to non‑capital offences, with a mandatory parliamentary review after two years (mirroring the 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam proportionality mandate). Stakeholder mapping includes the Supreme Court’s AI Committee, High Court registries, the Ministry of Law and Justice, civil‑liberty NGOs (e.g., Internet Freedom Foundation), and the Bar Council of India. Power asymmetry arises when proprietary vendors withhold model weights; the ethical decision template therefore requires an “Open‑Model Clause” in the procurement contract (GFR Rule 173‑iii) mandating source‑code escrow with the NIC. Option generation: (A) deploy a closed‑source commercial risk‑score engine; (B) develop an open‑source model trained on anonymised NJDG data under the Supreme Court’s supervision; (C) adopt a hybrid where the commercial engine runs on‑premise with full audit logs exported to the NJDG. Each option is scored on a “Judicial‑AI Trust Matrix” covering explainability (0‑5), bias‑audit frequency (months), human‑override compliance (%), and cost (₹ crore). The final speaking order must cite the IT Act 2000 §43A, DPDP Act 2023 §12, Supreme Court 2023 AI Guidelines, and the 2022 proportionality judgment.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Biometric Voter Authentication Systems

The Election Commission of India (ECI) has piloted biometric voter authentication — fingerprint and iris scans — in select constituencies under the Representation of the People Act 1951 (Section 61A) and the 2022 “Guidelines for Biometric Verification at Polling Stations”. The constitutional backdrop is the K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) judgment establishing informational privacy as a facet of Article 21, and the 2019 Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (Aadhaar) ruling that biometric collection must satisfy the triple test of legality, necessity, and proportionality. An ethical governance framework therefore imposes: (1) Legal Basis — a specific amendment to the Representation of the People Act authorising biometric capture, not merely an executive circular; (2) Purpose Limitation — data used solely for voter identity verification on polling day, with automatic deletion within 30 days (mirroring the Aadhaar Act 2016 §29); (3) Data Minimisation & Security — only encrypted template hashes stored on air‑gapped ECI servers; no raw images leave the polling booth; (4) Informed Consent & Opt‑Out — voters may choose alternative identity documents (EPIC, passport) without penalty; (5) Independent Audit — the CAG conducts a post‑election audit of biometric logs, and the Supreme Court’s 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam proportionality test applies to any retention beyond the statutory window. Stakeholder mapping includes the ECI, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), political parties, civil‑society groups (e.g., Association for Democratic Reforms), and voters. Power asymmetry appears when the ruling party pressures the ECI to expand biometric coverage without legislative sanction. The ethical decision template therefore requires a “Biometric‑Governance Matrix” specifying (a) legal authorisation, (b) data‑flow diagram, (c) deletion protocol, (d) grievance redressal mechanism (ECI’s “Voter Helpline 1950”). Options: (A) nationwide rollout under current executive guidelines; (B) pilot in 10 % of constituencies with a parliamentary bill for statutory backing; (C) retain existing EPIC‑only verification and defer biometrics until a comprehensive law is enacted. Each option is scored on a “Privacy‑Integrity‑Inclusivity” rubric (0‑5). The speaking order must reference the Representation of the People Act 1951 §61A, Aadhaar Act 2016 §29, Puttaswamy (2017), and the 2022 proportionality judgment.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Management of Cross‑Border Data Flows under Trade Agreements

India’s participation in digital trade chapters — such as the India‑Australia Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement (ECTA, 2022), the India‑UK Free Trade Agreement negotiations, and the WTO Joint Statement Initiative on E‑Commerce — creates obligations on cross‑border data flows that intersect with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act) and the Supreme Court’s K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) data‑localisation jurisprudence. An ethical framework for managing these flows rests on four pillars: (1) Sovereign Adequacy — any recipient jurisdiction must be assessed against the DPDP Act’s “adequacy” criteria (Section 16) before unrestricted transfer; (2) Purpose‑Bound Transfer — data shared under a trade agreement may only be processed for the specific commercial or regulatory purpose enumerated in the treaty annex; (3) Accountability & Redress — the data‑exporter (Indian public authority) remains liable for downstream breaches, enforceable through the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI) established under DPDP Act 2023; (4) Proportionality & Sunset Review — each data‑flow clause includes a mandatory review after three years, aligned with the 2022 State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam proportionality test. Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), the Department of Commerce, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for financial data, sectoral regulators (TRAI, IRDAI), foreign data‑importers, and civil‑society watchdogs (e.g., Software Freedom Law Centre). Power asymmetry arises when trade negotiators concede broad “free flow” language without sector‑specific safeguards. The ethical decision template therefore requires a “Cross‑Border Data‑Flow Matrix” that lists (a) data categories, (b) treaty provision, (c) adequacy assessment outcome, (d) contractual safeguards (standard contractual clauses, binding corporate rules), (e) audit schedule. Options: (A) adopt a blanket “free flow” commitment for all non‑sensitive data; (B) negotiate sector‑specific adequacy annexes with a “data‑localisation carve‑out” for health, finance, and biometric data; (C) retain the DPDP Act’s default restriction and only permit transfers via explicit DPBI‑approved adequacy decisions. Each option is scored on a “Sovereignty‑Trade‑Trust” triad (0‑5). The speaking order must cite DPDP Act 2023 §§12, 16, 27; the ECTA digital trade chapter; the WTO JSI e‑commerce moratorium; and the 2022 proportionality judgment.

  • Assuming that a blockchain pilot automatically guarantees procurement integrity without a CVC‑mandated post‑award audit and third‑party oracle verification.
  • Applying a pure utilitarian calculus to pandemic resource allocation while ignoring the prioritarian equity weights mandated by the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016.
  • Deploying an AI sentencing aid without a published bias‑audit report, an open‑model escrow clause, and a statutory human‑in‑the‑loop requirement.
  • Rolling out biometric voter authentication on the basis of an executive circular alone, bypassing the Representation of the People Act amendment and the Puttaswamy triple test.
  • Accepting a trade‑agreement “free flow” clause for health data without conducting a DPDP Act adequacy assessment and embedding a DPBI‑enforceable sunset review.
  • Failing to record a speaking order that cites the exact statutory provision, judicial precedent, and scoring matrix for every discretionary decision in the above domains.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Algorithmic Auditing for Procurement

Algorithmic auditing introduces a structured, repeatable check on the integrity of e‑procurement platforms. The General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, Rule 173, mandate that all high‑value tenders be processed through the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) and that an independent audit trail be maintained. An ethical framework for algorithmic auditing rests on three pillars: (1) Transparency of Logic – the scoring algorithm, weightage matrix, and exclusion criteria must be published in the tender document; (2) Independent Verification – a third‑party auditor empaneled by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) must run a parallel simulation on a sample of bids and certify that the automated ranking matches the manual evaluation; (3) Remediation Protocol – any discrepancy triggers a mandatory “audit‑pause” during which the procuring entity must publish a reasoned order, allow affected bidders to file representations under Section 7 of the Right to Information Act 2005, and rectify the algorithm before award.

Stakeholder mapping includes the procuring ministry, the CVC, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the GeM SPV, empaneled auditors, bidder associations (e.g., Confederation of Indian Industry), and civil‑society watchdogs such as Transparency International India. Power asymmetry arises when the procuring entity controls the algorithm’s source code and refuses external review citing “commercial confidentiality”. The ethical decision template therefore requires an Algorithmic‑Audit Matrix that records (a) algorithm version, (b) open‑source or escrow status, (c) auditor’s independence declaration, (d) discrepancy log, and (e) remediation timeline.

Options for a case where a high‑value defence procurement shows a 12 % ranking deviation: (A) accept the automated award and issue a post‑award audit report; (B) suspend award, commission an immediate CVC‑empaneled audit, and re‑run the evaluation with the corrected algorithm; (C) cancel the tender and re‑tender with a fully open‑source scoring engine. Scoring on a “Integrity‑Fairness‑Efficiency” rubric (0‑5) typically yields Option B as the defensible choice because it respects the GFR mandate for timely procurement while upholding the constitutional duty of fairness under Article 14. The speaking order must cite GFR 2017 Rule 173, CVC Circular 04/2020 on e‑procurement integrity, the Supreme Court judgment in State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2022) on proportionality, and the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order 2017.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Synthetic Media for Public Communication

Synthetic media — deep‑fake video, AI‑generated voice, and text‑to‑image outputs — are increasingly used by ministries for multilingual outreach, crisis alerts, and policy explainers. The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021, Rule 4(2), require that any “synthetic” content disseminated by a public authority carry a visible label stating “AI‑generated” and a link to the source model’s documentation. An ethical governance framework adds four safeguards: (1) Provenance Registry – each synthetic asset is logged in a ministry‑wide registry (hosted on the National Informatics Centre cloud) with hash, model version, training data licence, and responsible officer; (2) Human‑in‑the‑Loop Approval – a designated communications officer, cleared under the Official Secrets Act 1923, must sign off before publication; (3) Redress Mechanism – citizens can flag misleading synthetic content via the Grievance Appellate Committee established under the IT Rules 2021, triggering a 48‑hour takedown review; (4) Periodic Audit – the CVC conducts an annual audit of the registry to verify that no synthetic asset was used for political persuasion contrary to the Model Code of Conduct.

Stakeholders comprise the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, the Press Information Bureau, the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Election Commission of India (ECI), fact‑checking organisations (e.g., Alt News), and the general public. Power asymmetry is evident when a ruling party’s digital wing pressures the ministry to deploy synthetic avatars of leaders without the mandatory label. The decision template therefore uses a Synthetic‑Media Governance Matrix capturing (a) content type, (b) label compliance, (c) registry entry ID, (d) approval chain, (e) audit flag.

Options for a scenario where a health ministry releases an AI‑generated video of a minister urging vaccination without a label: (A) issue a retroactive label and publish an erratum; (B) withdraw the video, conduct a root‑cause analysis, and re‑release a compliant version after CVC clearance; (C) continue dissemination arguing “public interest” overrides labelling. Scoring on a “Transparency‑Accountability‑Public‑Trust” triad (0‑5) favours Option B, which aligns with the IT Rules 2021, the Supreme Court’s K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) privacy‑dignity jurisprudence, and the ECI’s 2022 advisory on synthetic media in elections. The speaking order must reference IT Rules 2021 Rule 4(2), the Official Secrets Act 1923 Section 5, the CVC Annual Report 2023 on synthetic media, and the ECI advisory dated 12 January 2022.

Technique: Synthetic‑Media Governance Matrix in a 15‑Mark Answer
A state health department releases an AI‑generated video of the Chief Minister urging citizens to adopt a new health insurance scheme. The video carries no “AI‑generated” label. As the Ethics Officer, outline the immediate steps, the governance matrix you would invoke, and the final decision with justification.
Step 1 – Immediate Containment: Order the video’s removal from all official channels within 2 hours; issue a public notice acknowledging the omission. Step 2 – Invoke Governance Matrix: Populate the Synthetic‑Media Governance Matrix: (a) Content = Video; (b) Label = Missing; (c) Registry ID = None (retro‑entry created); (d) Approval = Unsigned; (e) Audit = Flagged. Step 3 – Human‑in‑the‑Loop Review: Convene the designated communications officer, the CVC‑empaneled auditor, and the state’s Chief Information Commissioner. Step 4 – Decision: Choose Option B – withdraw, conduct root‑cause analysis, re‑release a labelled version after CVC clearance. Justification: Compliance with IT Rules 2021 Rule 4(2); upholds Article 14 fairness; preserves public trust per Puttaswamy (2017); satisfies ECI advisory on synthetic media. Speaking Order: Cite IT Rules 2021 Rule 4(2), Official Secrets Act 1923 §5, CVC Circular 04/2020, ECI Advisory 12 Jan 2022, and the matrix scores (Transparency 4, Accountability 5, Trust 4).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study mentions “AI‑generated” or “deep‑fake” content, instantly map the IT Rules 2021 labelling requirement, the CVC audit cycle, and the ECI advisory. Structure the answer in three moves: (1) containment, (2) matrix population, (3) scored option with speaking order. This pattern repeats across synthetic‑media, algorithmic‑audit, and predictive‑analytics cases, saving precious minutes.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Allocation of Emergency Powers during Health Crises

The Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 (Section 2) and the Disaster Management Act 2005 (Sections 30‑34) empower state governments to issue extraordinary orders — lockdowns, requisition of private hospitals, price caps on essential drugs — without prior legislative sanction. An ethical framework for invoking these powers must satisfy the Triple Test of Necessity, Proportionality, and Temporal Limitation derived from the Supreme Court’s State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2022) and the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. Necessity demands a real‑time epidemiological threshold (e.g., test‑positivity > 10 % for 14 consecutive days) certified by the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP). Proportionality requires that the restriction be the least intrusive measure achieving the public‑health objective; for instance, a night‑curfew is preferred over a full lockdown when the reproduction number (R) is below 1.5. Temporal limitation obliges the authority to embed a sunset clause — typically 21 days — with mandatory legislative ratification thereafter, as envisaged in the Disaster Management Act 2005 Section 35.

Stakeholder mapping includes the State Health Department, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), the State Legislative Assembly, the High Court (via suo‑motu PILs), civil‑society groups (e.g., Jan Swasthya Abhiyan), and affected citizens (especially migrant workers). Power asymmetry surfaces when the executive bypasses the legislative assembly and the judiciary by issuing successive 14‑day orders without debate. The decision template therefore employs an Emergency‑Powers Allocation Matrix recording (a) epidemiological trigger, (b) measure catalogue with intrusiveness score, (c) sunset date, (d) legislative ratification status, (e) judicial review docket number.

Options for a state facing a sudden surge: (A) impose a 30‑day complete lockdown via executive order; (B) issue a 14‑day graded restriction package (night curfew, capacity limits, mandatory masking) with a built‑in 21‑day sunset and a resolution for assembly ratification; (C) defer to central guidelines and request the NDMA to declare a national disaster. Scoring on a “Necessity‑Proportionality‑Democratic‑Legitimacy” rubric (0‑5) typically selects Option B, which respects the constitutional scheme, satisfies the proportionality test, and provides a clear accountability trail. The speaking order must cite Epidemic Diseases Act 1897 §2, Disaster Management Act 2005 §§30‑35, State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2022), and the NDMA’s 2021 “Guidelines for Graded Response”.

Applying the Principle of Non‑Discrimination in Public‑Sector AI‑Driven Eligibility Screening

AI‑driven eligibility engines — used for scholarship disbursement, subsidised housing allocation, and pension verification — must comply with the constitutional guarantee of equality under Article 15 and the statutory mandate of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (Section 3) which requires reasonable accommodation. The Supreme Court in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) affirmed that indirect discrimination is actionable when a neutral criterion disproportionately harms a protected group. An ethical screening framework therefore integrates three technical‑legal controls: (1) Bias‑Audit Registry – every model version undergoes an independent audit (empaneled by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology) that publishes disparate‑impact ratios for gender, caste, disability, and religion; (2) Explainability Layer – the engine must generate a human‑readable reason code for each rejection, enabling the applicant to invoke Section 7 of the Right to Information Act 2005; (3) Human‑Override Protocol – a designated grievance officer, appointed under the Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism (PGRM) 2020, can overturn an automated denial within 15 days after a reasoned order.

Stakeholders comprise the implementing ministry (e.g., Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment), the National Informatics Centre (NIC) as platform host, the empaneled auditors, the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, the National Commission for Women, disability rights organisations (e.g., National Centre for Promotion of Employment for Disabled People), and the applicant community. Power asymmetry arises when the model’s training data reflects historic exclusion (e.g., land‑ownership records biased against Scheduled Tribes) and the ministry refuses to disclose the feature set citing “algorithmic secrecy”. The decision template uses a Non‑Discrimination Screening Matrix capturing (a) protected attributes tested, (b) disparate‑impact threshold (≤ 0.8), (c) explainability score (0‑5), (d) override utilisation rate, (e) audit cycle date.

Options for a scholarship portal that rejects 22 % of eligible Scheduled Tribe applicants due to a “digital‑literacy” proxy variable: (A) retain the model, publish a generic FAQ; (B) suspend the proxy, re‑train with inclusive features, conduct a fresh bias audit, and deploy the human‑override for pending cases; (C) abandon AI screening and revert to manual verification. Scoring on an “Equality‑Transparency‑Efficiency” triad (0‑5) favours Option B, which aligns with Article 15, the RPwD Act 2016, Navtej Singh Johar (2018), and the MeitY “Responsible AI for Social Empowerment” (RAISE) 2022 guidelines. The speaking order must reference Constitution Article 15, RPwD Act 2016 §3, RTI Act 2005 §7, Navtej Singh Johar (2018), and the RAISE 2022 framework.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Digital Identity for Social Protection Portability

Portable digital identity — enabling a migrant worker to access food‑security benefits, health insurance, and pension contributions across state borders — rests on the Aadhaar Act 2016 (Section 7) and the recently enacted Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act, Sections 12‑13). The Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) held that any mandatory linkage must satisfy the triple test of legality, necessity, and proportionality. An ethical governance architecture for portability therefore comprises four layers: (1) Consent‑Centred Architecture – the beneficiary provides explicit, revocable consent for each data‑sharing transaction via the DPDP‑compliant consent artefact; (2) Inter‑State Data‑Sharing Agreement (ISDSA) – a memorandum of understanding between state governments, vetted by the Ministry of Home Affairs, specifying purpose‑bound fields, retention periods, and audit logs; (3) Grievance Redressal Hub – a single‑window portal (integrated with the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System, CPGRAMS) where a beneficiary can challenge erroneous de‑duplication or denial; (4) Independent Audit & Sunset Review – the CAG conducts a biennial audit of the ISDSA, and each agreement expires after five years unless renewed by legislative resolution.

Stakeholder mapping includes the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), state Departments of Food & Civil Supplies, Health, and Labour, the Ministry of Labour & Employment, the National Health Authority (NHA), the Comptroller and Auditor General, civil‑society groups (e.g., Right to Food Campaign), and the migrant worker collectives. Power asymmetry appears when a receiving state demands full Aadhaar‑based authentication without offering the consent artefact, effectively coercing the worker. The decision template employs a Portability Governance Matrix recording (a) data fields shared, (b) consent artefact ID, (c) ISDSA clause reference, (d) grievance ticket SLA, (e) audit schedule.

Options for a scenario where a construction worker from Bihar is denied ration in Maharashtra because the state insists on biometric authentication without a consent record: (A) allow authentication on the spot and create a retroactive consent log; (B) deny service until a proper ISDSA and consent artefact are in place, while providing an interim cash transfer via the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) platform; (C) escalate to the Supreme Court for a mandamus. Scoring on a “Consent‑Portability‑Accountability” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, which respects the DPDP Act’s consent requirement, upholds the proportionality test from Puttaswamy (2017), and provides a safety‑net through DBT. The speaking order must cite Aadhaar Act 2016 §7, DPDP Act 2023 §§12‑13, K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), the CAG’s 2022 report on inter‑state benefit portability, and the DBT framework under the Public Financial Management System.

  • Assuming that a single algorithmic audit certifies a procurement platform for all future tenders without periodic re‑audit.
  • Treating synthetic‑media labelling as optional when the content is “informational” rather than “political”.
  • Invoking emergency powers under the Epidemic Diseases Act without a documented epidemiological trigger and sunset clause.
  • Deploying an AI eligibility engine that uses proxy variables (e.g., digital‑literacy) without a published disparate‑impact audit.
  • Allowing a state to demand full Aadhaar authentication for portable benefits without a DPDP‑compliant consent artefact and an inter‑state data‑sharing agreement.
  • Failing to embed a human‑override protocol and a grievance‑redressal SLA in every automated decision‑making system used for public‑service delivery.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Algorithmic Risk Scoring for Child Protection Services

Child protection agencies increasingly deploy algorithmic risk‑scoring tools to prioritise investigations, allocate caseworkers, and predict recurrence of abuse. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 mandates that the best interests of the child be the paramount consideration, while the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 imposes stringent reporting duties. Any automated system must therefore satisfy the constitutional test of proportionality articulated in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — legality, necessity, and proportionality — and the statutory requirement of procedural fairness under Section 19 of the Juvenile Justice Act.

A robust governance framework comprises four layers. First, a model‑validation mandate requiring an independent audit of training data for representativeness across caste, religion, disability, and geographic dimensions, documented in a publicly accessible model‑card. Second, a human‑in‑the‑loop protocol that obliges a qualified child‑welfare officer to review every high‑risk score before any investigative action, with a recorded rationale. Third, a grievance‑redressal channel integrated with the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) portal, allowing families to contest scores within 30 days and trigger a mandatory re‑assessment. Fourth, a periodic impact review every 12 months, published by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, measuring false‑positive rates, disparate impact indices, and outcomes for children placed in alternative care.

Stakeholder mapping reveals hidden power asymmetries: the algorithm vendor holds proprietary code, the state child‑protection department controls case allocation, and families often lack digital literacy to challenge decisions. The decision template uses a Risk‑Score Governance Matrix capturing (a) data sources, (b) feature list, (c) audit reference, (d) human‑review SLA, (e) grievance‑ticket ID, and (f) review‑cycle date. Options for a scenario where a model flags a tribal household solely on a proxy variable “distance to health centre” are: (A) accept the score and initiate investigation; (B) suspend the proxy, retrain with culturally sensitive features, and deploy the human‑override for pending cases; (C) abandon the model and revert to manual triage. Scoring on a “Best‑Interest‑Transparency‑Equity” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, aligning with Article 15(3), the Juvenile Justice Act 2015 § 3, and the MeitY “Responsible AI for Social Empowerment” (RAISE) 2022 guidelines.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Deployment of AI‑Enabled Traffic Management Systems

Smart‑city missions across states have introduced AI‑driven adaptive signal control, incident detection, and dynamic lane‑allocation to reduce congestion and emissions. The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (as amended 2019) empowers the Central Government to prescribe standards for electronic traffic regulation, while the Information Technology Act, 2000 (Section 43A) imposes a duty of reasonable security for personal data captured by cameras and sensors. The Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) extended the right to privacy to movement data, requiring any surveillance to meet the triple test of legality, necessity, and proportionality.

An ethical governance architecture for such systems rests on five pillars. (1) Purpose‑Limited Data Collection — only vehicle‑count, speed, and occupancy metrics are stored; licence‑plate images are hashed and discarded after 24 hours unless a verified incident triggers retention under the Criminal Procedure Code. (2) Algorithmic Transparency Register — each deployed model is listed in a public register maintained by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, with version, training‑data provenance, and performance metrics (precision, recall, demographic parity). (3) Independent Bias Audit — an empanelled third‑party auditor evaluates disparate impact across vehicle‑type, neighbourhood income, and time‑of‑day before each major release, publishing a summary report. (4) Human‑Override & Escalation — traffic‑control operators retain authority to suspend automated phase‑changes during emergencies, with a logged justification. (5) Citizen Feedback Loop — a mobile‑app channel lets commuters report erroneous signal behaviour, feeding a continuous‑learning pipeline subject to the same audit cycle.

Stakeholder mapping includes the National Highways Authority of India, state transport departments, city municipal corporations, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, civil‑society groups such as the Internet Freedom Foundation, and commuter associations. Power asymmetry arises when a vendor’s proprietary optimisation objective (e.g., maximising throughput) conflicts with equitable access for non‑motorised users. The decision template employs a Traffic‑AI Governance Scorecard recording (a) data‑retention policy, (b) audit‑report reference, (c) human‑override SLA, (d) feedback‑resolution time, (e) equity‑impact index. Options for a scenario where an adaptive‑signal system consistently prioritises arterial roads, starving residential lanes of green time: (A) retain current optimisation and issue a public notice; (B) re‑weight the objective function to include a minimum‑green‑time constraint for all lanes, commission a fresh bias audit, and publish the revised model card; (C) revert to fixed‑time plans city‑wide. Scoring on an “Equity‑Efficiency‑Accountability” triad (0‑5) favours Option B, satisfying the Motor Vehicles Act 2019 § 138, the IT Act 2000 § 43A, and the RAISE 2022 fairness principles.

Worked Illustration: Stakeholder Impact Matrix
A municipal corporation proposes an AI‑based predictive policing module that assigns patrol intensity scores to wards using historic crime data, 911 call logs, and socio‑economic indicators. Identify the three most critical ethical risks and propose a mitigation for each, citing the relevant legal anchor.
Risk 1 – Historical Bias Amplification. Historic crime data over‑represents policing in marginalised neighbourhoods, leading to a feedback loop. Mitigation: Conduct a disparate‑impact audit per the RAISE 2022 framework; re‑weight features to satisfy demographic parity; legal anchor — Article 14 (equality) and K.S. Puttaswamy (proportionality).
Risk 2 – Absence of Human‑Override. Automated patrol allocation may dispatch officers without supervisory review. Mitigation: Mandate a senior officer sign‑off for any ward scoring above the 80th percentile; legal anchor — Section 149 CrPC (preventive action) read with the duty of procedural fairness.
Risk 3 – Data‑Retention Beyond Purpose. Call‑logs and location traces retained indefinitely. Mitigation: Enforce a 90‑day auto‑purge policy with audit logs; legal anchor — IT Act 2000 § 43A and the DPDP Act 2023 §§ 12‑13 (purpose limitation).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a case study asks for an “ethical governance architecture”, first list the statutory anchors (Act, Section, landmark judgment) in a single sentence. Then structure the answer as numbered pillars — each pillar = one paragraph — ending with a decision matrix that scores options on a named rubric. This pattern signals to the examiner that you have a repeatable method and can apply it under time pressure.

Ethical Frameworks for Public‑Sector Allocation of Resources for Community Mental Health Programs

The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 guarantees the right to access mental health care and mandates that the State allocate sufficient funds for community‑based services. The National Mental Health Policy (2014) and the Sustainable Development Goal 3.4 set targets for reducing premature mortality from mental disorders. However, budgetary constraints often force trade‑offs between institutional care, tele‑psychiatry, and community outreach. An ethical allocation framework must operationalise the principles of substantive equality, participatory budgeting, and intergenerational equity.

Four operational pillars guide resource decisions. (1) Needs‑Based Equity Index — a composite metric combining prevalence data (National Mental Health Survey 2015‑16), treatment‑gap ratios, and socio‑economic deprivation scores (SECC 2011). Districts scoring above the 75th percentile receive a minimum 30 % uplift in per‑capita allocation. (2) Participatory Allocation Committees — each district constitutes a committee with representation from service users, caregivers, NGOs, and the District Mental Health Programme officer; decisions are recorded in a public ledger. (3) Outcome‑Linked Funding — a portion (15 %) of the budget is released only after verified improvements in key indicators (e.g., reduction in involuntary admissions, increase in community‑based follow‑up). (4) Sunset Review & Intergenerational Audit — every five years the Comptroller and Auditor General conducts an audit assessing long‑term sustainability, workforce capacity, and impact on future cohorts, with findings tabled in the State Legislature.

Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, State Health Societies, the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), civil‑society networks such as the Mariwala Health Initiative, and service‑user collectives. Power asymmetry appears when tertiary hospitals lobby for larger shares, marginalising primary‑care NGOs. The decision template uses a Mental‑Health Resource Allocation Matrix capturing (a) district equity index, (b) committee minutes reference, (c) outcome‑milestone tracker, (d) audit schedule. Options for a scenario where a state proposes to divert 40 % of community‑outreach funds to a new tertiary centre: (A) approve the diversion with a promise to revisit in two years; (B) reject the diversion, enforce the equity‑index floor, and redirect the funds to tele‑psychiatry hubs in underserved blocks; (C) split the amount equally between the centre and outreach. Scoring on an “Equity‑Effectiveness‑Sustainability” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, consistent with the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 § 18, the National Mental Health Policy 2014, and the CAG’s 2021 performance audit on mental health spending.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Use of Citizen‑Generated Data for Urban Planning

Smart‑city initiatives increasingly ingest crowdsourced data — mobile‑app pothole reports, air‑quality sensor feeds from resident associations, and participatory GIS mappings — to inform master‑plan revisions. The Right to Information Act, 2005 (Section 4) obliges proactive disclosure of planning data, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Sections 12‑13) requires explicit, revocable consent for personal data processing. The Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) affirmed that data generated in public spaces retains a reasonable expectation of privacy when linked to identifiable individuals.

An ethical governance model for citizen‑generated data rests on three safeguards. (1) Consent‑Layer Architecture — each data‑submission interface presents a granular consent artefact specifying purpose, retention period, and sharing scope; the artefact is stored on a DPDP‑compliant consent manager. (2) Data‑Quality & Representativeness Audit — before integration, an independent statistician evaluates coverage bias (e.g., smartphone penetration gaps across income quintiles) and publishes a bias‑report card. (3) Deliberative Validation Forum — a quarterly multi‑stakeholder forum (urban local body, ward committees, academia, digital‑rights NGOs) reviews the analytical outputs, endorses or requests re‑analysis, and records dissenting views in the plan‑revision dossier.

Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, city municipal corporations, the National Informatics Centre, the Data Protection Board, resident‑welfare associations, and informal‑settlement federations. Power asymmetry emerges when high‑income neighbourhoods generate dense sensor streams, skewing infrastructure prioritisation. The decision template employs a Citizen‑Data Governance Scorecard recording (a) consent‑artefact ID, (b) bias‑report reference, (c) forum‑minutes link, (d) data‑retention schedule, (e) grievance‑redressal SLA. Options for a scenario where a flood‑risk model built on crowdsourced elevation points excludes a low‑lying slum because residents lack smartphones: (A) publish the model with a disclaimer; (B) commission a targeted ground‑survey, augment the dataset, re‑run the model, and present both versions at the validation forum; (C) discard crowdsourced data and rely solely on satellite‑derived DEM. Scoring on a “Inclusivity‑Reliability‑Accountability” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, aligning with the RTI Act 2005 § 4, DPDP Act 2023 §§ 12‑13, and the National Urban Innovation Stack (NUIS) 2022 guidelines.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Use of Biometric Authentication for Border Control Operations

Border agencies are piloting multimodal biometric gates — iris, fingerprint, and facial recognition — to expedite passenger clearance. The Citizenship Act, 1955 (Section 14A) authorises the Central Government to prescribe biometric collection for identity verification, while the Aadhaar Act, 2016 (Section 7) limits mandatory authentication to subsidies and services. The Supreme Court in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) held that any biometric mandate must satisfy legality, necessity, and proportionality, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Sections 12‑13) imposes purpose‑limitation and consent requirements even for state functions.

A proportionate governance framework comprises four controls. (1) Legal‑Basis Register — each biometric modality is mapped to a specific statutory provision (e.g., iris for e‑Visa holders under the Passport Act, 1967; fingerprint for deportation orders under the Foreigners Act, 1946). (2) Minimal‑Data Capture Principle — only the biometric template required for the declared purpose is stored; raw images are discarded within 24 hours. (3) Independent Algorithmic Audit — the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) conducts an annual audit of false‑match rates disaggregated by age, ethnicity, and disability, publishing a summary. (4) Human‑Review & Redressal — a designated immigration officer must verify any automated rejection; the traveller can file a grievance via the CPGRAMS portal with a 48‑hour SLA.

Stakeholder mapping includes the Bureau of Immigration, Ministry of Home Affairs, Unique Identification Authority of India, National Crime Records Bureau, civil‑liberties organisations such as the Human Rights Law Network, and traveller‑association groups. Power asymmetry arises when a vendor’s proprietary matching algorithm is treated as a black box, preventing effective oversight. The decision template uses a Border‑Biometric Governance Matrix capturing (a) legal‑basis citation, (b) data‑retention policy, (c) audit‑report reference, (d) human‑review SLA, (e) grievance‑ticket ID. Options for a scenario where a facial‑recognition gate repeatedly flags travellers from a specific ethnic group for secondary screening: (A) increase the confidence threshold globally; (B) suspend the facial modality, commission an urgent disparate‑impact audit, and revert to fingerprint‑only verification pending remediation; (C) retain the system and issue a public advisory. Scoring on a “Proportionality‑Non‑Discrimination‑Accountability” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, consistent with Article 14, the Citizenship Act 1955 § 14A, the Aadhaar Act 2016 § 7, and the DPDP Act 2023 §§ 12‑13.

  • Assuming a single algorithmic audit certifies a system for all future deployments without periodic re‑audit.
  • Treating synthetic‑media labelling as optional when the content is labelled “informational” rather than “political”.
  • Invoking emergency powers under the Epidemic Diseases Act without a documented epidemiological trigger and sunset clause.
  • Deploying an AI eligibility engine that uses proxy variables such as digital‑literacy without a published disparate‑impact audit.
  • Allowing a state to demand full Aadhaar authentication for portable benefits without a DPDP‑compliant consent artefact and an inter‑state data‑sharing agreement.
  • Failing to embed a human‑override protocol and a grievance‑redressal SLA in every automated decision‑making system used for public‑service delivery.
  • Neglecting to conduct a representativeness audit of citizen‑generated data before integrating it into master‑plan revisions.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Public‑Sector Algorithmic Risk Scoring for Child Protection Services

Child protection agencies increasingly deploy algorithmic risk‑scoring tools to prioritise investigations, allocate caseworkers, and predict recurrence of abuse. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 mandates that the best interests of the child be the paramount consideration, while the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) impose obligations of purpose limitation, data minimisation, and consent for any processing of children’s personal data. A proportionate governance framework for such tools rests on four pillars.

1. Legal‑Basis Register. Each model must be linked to a specific statutory provision — for example, Section 27 of the Juvenile Justice Act authorises the Child Welfare Committee to order inquiries; the model’s output can only inform, not replace, that statutory discretion. The register records the exact legal clause, the data categories ingested (police FIRs, school attendance, health records), and the retention schedule (maximum 24 months unless a court order extends it).

2. Bias‑Impact Audit. Before deployment, an independent audit — preferably by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy or an empanelled academic centre — must publish disparate‑impact metrics disaggregated by caste, religion, gender, disability, and geographic region. The audit follows the “Fairness‑Accountability‑Transparency” (FAT) checklist endorsed by NITI Aayog’s Responsible AI for Social Empowerment (RAISE) 2022 guidelines. Any metric exceeding a 10 % adverse‑impact threshold triggers a mandatory model‑re‑training cycle.

3. Human‑in‑the‑Loop Protocol. The algorithm produces a risk score; a designated Child Protection Officer (CPO) must review every score above a calibrated threshold before any field action. The CPO documents the rationale for acceptance or override in a case‑management system that is auditable under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The protocol also requires a 48‑hour grievance‑redressal window for families, accessible via the CPGRAMS portal.

4. Continuous Monitoring & Sunset Review. A quarterly dashboard tracks false‑positive rates, case‑closure outcomes, and any emergent bias. After two years, a sunset review — mandated by the DPDP Act § 12(2) — decides whether the tool continues, is modified, or is retired. The review panel includes a representative from the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR), a data‑protection officer, and a civil‑society member.

Stakeholder mapping reveals a power asymmetry: the vendor’s proprietary model is often a black box, while frontline caseworkers lack technical literacy to challenge scores. The decision template therefore captures (a) legal‑basis citation, (b) bias‑audit reference, (c) human‑review log ID, (d) grievance‑ticket number, and (e) sunset‑review minutes. Options for a scenario where a model flags a disproportionate number of Scheduled‑Tribe families in a tribal district: (A) lower the threshold uniformly; (B) suspend the model for that district, commission a targeted bias audit, and revert to manual triage pending remediation; (C) continue with a public disclaimer. Scoring on a “Best‑Interest‑Non‑Discrimination‑Accountability” rubric (0‑5) selects Option B, aligning with Article 15(4), the Juvenile Justice Act, and DPDP Act §§ 12‑13.

Ethical Governance of Public‑Sector Remote Sensing Data for Land‑Use Monitoring

Remote sensing — satellite imagery, aerial LiDAR, and drone‑borne multispectral data — underpins land‑use planning, forest‑cover verification, and enforcement of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) and the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR). The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) operate under the Space Activities Bill, 2017 (draft) and the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 (for spectrum). Ethical governance must reconcile three imperatives: scientific accuracy, tenure security for forest‑dwelling communities, and procedural fairness.

1. Data‑Provenance Ledger. Every dataset entering a land‑use decision is logged with sensor metadata (resolution, acquisition date, atmospheric correction), processing chain (orthorectification, classification algorithm version), and licensing terms (open‑data vs. commercial licence). The ledger is stored on a tamper‑evident registry (e.g., a blockchain‑anchored hash) to satisfy the evidentiary standards of the Supreme Court in Orissa Mining Corp. v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013).

2. Community‑Ground‑Truthing Protocol. Before a classification map is used to demarcate “forest land” or “wasteland”, a mandatory ground‑truthing exercise involves Gram Sabha representatives, Joint Forest Management Committee members, and an independent geospatial auditor. The protocol follows the FRA’s requirement of “free, prior and informed consent” (FPIC) for any diversion of forest land. Discrepancies between satellite‑derived classes and community‑verified boundaries are recorded in a Conflict‑Resolution Register.

3. Proportionality‑Based Access Controls. High‑resolution (< 0.5 m) imagery that can identify individual dwellings is classified as “sensitive spatial data” under the National Geospatial Policy, 2022. Access is granted only to authorised officers with a written justification linked to a specific statutory function (e.g., Section 4 of LARR for social impact assessment). All accesses are logged and subject to quarterly audit by the State Remote Sensing Application Centre.

4. Transparent Decision‑Audit Trail. When a land‑use change (e.g., conversion of “forest” to “non‑forest”) is approved, the decision file must attach (a) the satellite‑derived map version, (b) the ground‑truthing minutes, (c) the proportionality assessment (necessity, least‑intrusive alternative), and (d) the Gram Sabha resolution. This trail enables judicial review under Article 226 and satisfies the “public trust” doctrine articulated in M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1997).

Stakeholder mapping includes the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC), State Revenue Departments, ISRO/NRSC, tribal rights NGOs (e.g., Campaign for Survival and Dignity), and private agribusiness firms. Power asymmetry arises when commercial firms obtain high‑resolution data through licences that bypass community consent. The decision template captures (a) data‑provenance hash, (b) ground‑truthing report ID, (c) access‑control log reference, (d) Gram Sabha resolution number, (e) proportionality‑assessment memo. Options for a case where a mining lease is granted based on a satellite map that misclassifies a tribal shifting‑cultivation area as “degraded forest”: (A) approve lease with a condition to re‑survey; (B) suspend lease, order joint ground‑truthing with Gram Sabha, and re‑evaluate classification; (C) reject lease outright.
